title: The Case of the Chute That Stopped Squeaking
story: Three odd things turned up in the library in the same week. Books returned through the outside drop chute arrive with curled, wavy pages. The carpet under the chute has a dark square the size of a doormat. And the brass chute flap, which squeaked for nine years, has gone completely silent. Rain blowing in through the chute would curl the pages, but rain cannot silence a flap. The wet bags readers carry in would mark the whole entrance, not one square under the chute. The reading room humidifier runs on the far side of the building behind two closed doors. A drinks spill soaks the carpet once and dries within a day, and this square has stayed dark since Monday. The flap's return spring snapped on Sunday night, and the flap now hangs open. A flap that rests open never swings, so it cannot squeak. An open chute lets night air and rain straight down onto the books below. It also lets that wet air settle on one square of carpet and keep it damp. The caretaker has not touched the carpet or the chute since the complaints began.
q: What is behind all three problems?

sus.why: the flap's return spring snapped on Sunday night, and the flap now hangs open
rain blowing in through the chute would curl the pages, but rain cannot silence a flap
the wet bags readers carry in would mark the whole entrance, not one square under the chute
the reading room humidifier runs on the far side of the building behind two closed doors
a drinks spill soaks the carpet once and dries within a day

ans: A snapped spring has left the chute flap hanging open.
proof: “The flap's return spring snapped on Sunday night, and the flap now hangs open.”
“A flap that rests open never swings, so it cannot squeak.”
“An open chute lets night air and rain straight down onto the books below.”
clears: Rain: “rain cannot silence a flap.”
Wet bags: “would mark the whole entrance, not one square under the chute.”
The humidifier: “runs on the far side of the building behind two closed doors.”
A spill: “soaks the carpet once and dries within a day, and this square has stayed dark since Monday.”
explain: Rain can curl pages. A spill can darken carpet. Neither can quiet a hinge. Only one thing in the case sits upstream of all three: a flap stuck open stops swinging, lets the weather in, and holds damp air over the square beneath it. When a single cause accounts for three symptoms that look unrelated, that is the cause.

d.story: Three odd things turned up in the library in the same week. Books from the outside drop chute arrive with curled, wavy pages. The carpet under the chute has a dark square the size of a doormat. And the brass flap, which squeaked for nine years, has gone silent. The flap's return spring snapped on Sunday night, and the flap now hangs open. A flap resting open never swings, and an open chute lets rain fall straight onto the books. Rain has fallen on six of the last seven days, the wettest week since March. Water running down the inside of the chute swells the flap's hinge and holds it still. Readers queue at the chute in wet coats and set streaming bags down on that square. The bag pile has stood there since Monday and the square has never had a chance to dry. Wet wool against brass leaves a film, and a filmed hinge slides without a sound. The humidifier was taken out of the reading room in September and returned to the store. No drink has been allowed past the entrance desk since the new rule in October.
d.q: What is behind all three problems? Pick one cause and prove it from the text.

sus.why: a spring that snapped on Sunday, leaving the flap hanging open
six wet days out of seven, with water running down inside the chute
wet coats and streaming bags set down on that square since Monday
a humidifier that left the reading room in September
drinks stopped at the entrance desk since October

evidence: “The flap's return spring snapped on Sunday night, and the flap now hangs open.”
“A flap resting open never swings, and an open chute lets rain fall straight onto the books.”
args.against: “Wet wool against brass leaves a film, and a filmed hinge slides without a sound.”

evidence: “Rain has fallen on six of the last seven days, the wettest week since March.”
“Water running down the inside of the chute swells the flap's hinge and holds it still.”
args.against: “The flap's return spring snapped on Sunday night, and the flap now hangs open.”

evidence: “Readers queue at the chute in wet coats and set streaming bags down on that square.”
“The bag pile has stood there since Monday and the square has never had a chance to dry.”
args.against: “Books from the outside drop chute arrive with curled, wavy pages.”

clears: The humidifier: “The humidifier was taken out of the reading room in September and returned to the store.”
A drinks spill: “No drink has been allowed past the entrance desk since the new rule in October.”
d.note: The solve version gave the spring the only route to a silent flap. Here rain swells the hinge and wet wool films it, so three causes reach the silence. Watch for the student who notices that the bag pile explains the carpet best and the pages worst, and has to decide whether that costs it the case.

title: The Case of the Ice Pack That Never Melted
story: Dev's yogurt is warm by lunchtime every day this term. Two other things go with it, and nobody has put them together. His ice pack is still frozen rock hard at noon. The outside of his bag is cold to the touch when he lifts it off the rack. A freezer that failed overnight would send out a soft ice pack, and his comes out solid. Worn insulation would let the cold leak out, so the pack would be melting faster, not slower. The radiator by the bag rack would warm the bag from the outside, and the outside is the cold part. A pack too small for the box would still sweat and soften by noon. Since Dev got the new bag in September, he has clipped the ice pack into the outside mesh pocket. There is a zipped insulated wall between that pocket and the food. The pack has been chilling the outer shell and the air around it all morning. Nothing cold has been inside the box with the yogurt since term began. An ice pack with no warm food beside it has almost nothing to melt it.
q: Why is the yogurt warm?

sus.who: 🧊 The pack in the outside pocket
sus.why: he has clipped the ice pack into the outside mesh pocket, with an insulated wall between it and the food
a freezer that failed overnight would send out a soft ice pack, and his comes out solid
worn insulation would let the cold leak out, so the pack would be melting faster, not slower
the radiator would warm the bag from the outside, and the outside is the cold part
a pack too small for the box would still sweat and soften by noon

ans: The ice pack is clipped outside the insulated wall, not inside with the food.
proof: “There is a zipped insulated wall between that pocket and the food.”
“Nothing cold has been inside the box with the yogurt since term began.”
“An ice pack with no warm food beside it has almost nothing to melt it.”
clears: A failed freezer: “a freezer that failed overnight would send out a soft ice pack, and his comes out solid.”
Worn insulation: “the pack would be melting faster, not slower.”
The radiator: “would warm the bag from the outside, and the outside is the cold part.”
A small pack: “a pack too small for the box would still sweat and soften by noon.”
explain: Warm yogurt alone has four plausible causes. Add the pack that will not melt and the shell that is cold, and only one survives. The cold is on the wrong side of the insulation, which is why the food never gets it and the pack never spends it. Three facts, one place they all come from.

d.story: Dev's yogurt is warm by lunchtime every day this term. Two things go with it that nobody has put beside it. His ice pack is still frozen rock hard at noon, and the outside of the bag is cold to the touch. Since September the pack has been clipped into the outside mesh pocket, behind a zipped insulated wall. Nothing cold has been inside the box with the food since term began. The bag's inner lining has split along the seam nearest that pocket. Cold escaping through a split reaches the shell and chills the fabric instead of the box. Fabric held near freezing all morning takes very little back from the pack beside it. The bag hangs on the rack with its food side against the radiator and its mesh side to the corridor. The radiator runs from seven until nine every morning of term. Corridor air by that door measures four degrees, colder than the staff room fridge. The freezer was serviced in August and holds minus twenty every night. The pack is the large size, cut to fill the whole width of the box.
d.q: Why is the yogurt warm? Choose one cause and quote the story.

sus.who: 🧊 The pack in the outside pocket
sus.why: clipped outside a zipped insulated wall since September
a freezer serviced in August, holding minus twenty
an inner lining split along the seam nearest the pocket
the food side against a radiator that runs seven until nine
a pack cut to fill the whole width of the box

evidence: “Since September the pack has been clipped into the outside mesh pocket, behind a zipped insulated wall.”
“Nothing cold has been inside the box with the food since term began.”
args.against: “The radiator runs from seven until nine every morning of term.”

evidence: “The bag's inner lining has split along the seam nearest that pocket.”
“Cold escaping through a split reaches the shell and chills the fabric instead of the box.”
args.against: “Fabric held near freezing all morning takes very little back from the pack beside it.”

evidence: “The bag hangs on the rack with its food side against the radiator and its mesh side to the corridor.”
“Corridor air by that door measures four degrees, colder than the staff room fridge.”
args.against: “Nothing cold has been inside the box with the food since term began.”

clears: A failed freezer: “The freezer was serviced in August and holds minus twenty every night.”
A pack too small: “The pack is the large size, cut to fill the whole width of the box.”
d.note: All three live answers put the cold on one side of a wall and the food on the other; they disagree about which wall. The radiator argument is the strongest on the facts and the weakest on timing, because the radiator stops at nine and the yogurt is warm at noon. That gap is worth the whole lesson.

title: The Case of the Pencils That Snapped Every Time
story: Lia cannot keep a point on a pencil for a single paragraph. Three facts sit beside the snapping, and each has been shrugged off on its own. The wooden barrels of her pencils have hairline splits running along the grain. A pencil from the same box, kept in Omar's tray, has written all week without breaking. Cheap pencils would fail for Omar too, and his came out of Lia's box. A blunt sharpener blade tears the wood at the tip and leaves the lead below it whole. Pressing too hard snaps a point at the paper, not three centimetres inside the wood. Lia carries her pencil case clipped to the outside of her rucksack, and it hits the stair rail every morning. A dropped case cracks the lead along its whole length inside the unbroken wood. It also splits the barrel along the grain, which is where wood gives way first. A lead cracked end to end has a break waiting wherever the sharpener happens to stop. Omar's pencil has never been in that case.
q: Why do Lia's pencils break and Omar's does not?

sus.who: 🎒 The case banging the stair rail
sus.why: she carries her pencil case clipped to the outside of her rucksack, and it hits the stair rail every morning
cheap pencils would fail for Omar too, and his came out of Lia's box
a blunt sharpener blade tears the wood at the tip and leaves the lead below it whole
pressing too hard snaps a point at the paper, not three centimetres inside the wood

ans: The pencil case is knocked against the stair rail every morning.
proof: “A dropped case cracks the lead along its whole length inside the unbroken wood.”
“It also splits the barrel along the grain, which is where wood gives way first.”
“A lead cracked end to end has a break waiting wherever the sharpener happens to stop.”
clears: Cheap pencils: “cheap pencils would fail for Omar too, and his came out of Lia's box.”
The sharpener: “a blunt sharpener blade tears the wood at the tip and leaves the lead below it whole.”
Pressing hard: “pressing too hard snaps a point at the paper, not three centimetres inside the wood.”
explain: The snapping has three companions: split barrels, a twin pencil that works, and breaks deep inside the wood. A bad batch cannot explain Omar's. A bad blade cannot explain the splits. Only the daily knock reaches all of it, because it damages the lead and the wood at once, everywhere along their length.

d.story: Lia cannot keep a point on a pencil for a single paragraph. Three facts sit beside the snapping and each has been shrugged off alone. The wooden barrels of her pencils have hairline splits running along the grain. The breaks happen three centimetres inside the wood, not at the paper. And a pencil from Omar's tray has written all week without breaking. Lia's pencil case is clipped to the outside of her rucksack and hits the stair rail every morning. A dropped case cracks the lead end to end inside wood that still looks whole. Lia's box came from the market stall and Omar's came from the school shop. Pencils glued badly at the factory split along the grain as the glue dries out. Lia presses hard enough to emboss the next three pages of her book. A lead squeezed by a grip that heavy breaks at its weakest point, wherever that happens to be. The sharpener was replaced with a new one on Monday and the snapping has not changed.
d.q: Why do Lia's pencils break and Omar's does not? Pick a cause and prove it.

sus.why: a case clipped outside the rucksack that hits the stair rail daily
a market stall box, where Omar's came from the school shop
a sharpener replaced on Monday
a grip heavy enough to emboss three pages ahead

evidence: “Lia's pencil case is clipped to the outside of her rucksack and hits the stair rail every morning.”
“A dropped case cracks the lead end to end inside wood that still looks whole.”
args.against: “The wooden barrels of her pencils have hairline splits running along the grain.”

evidence: “Lia's box came from the market stall and Omar's came from the school shop.”
“Pencils glued badly at the factory split along the grain as the glue dries out.”
args.against: “The breaks happen three centimetres inside the wood, not at the paper.”

evidence: “Lia presses hard enough to emboss the next three pages of her book.”
“A lead squeezed by a grip that heavy breaks at its weakest point, wherever that happens to be.”
args.against: “A dropped case cracks the lead end to end inside wood that still looks whole.”

clears: The sharpener: “The sharpener was replaced with a new one on Monday and the snapping has not changed.”
d.note: In the solve version Omar's pencil came out of Lia's box, which killed the batch answer outright. Two shops put it back on the table, and the split barrels now have a factory explanation as good as the stair rail one. Pressing hard is the weakest of the three and the one most students pick first.

title: The Case of the Tuesday Apples
story: Apples from the Tuesday crate bruise within a day of reaching the classrooms. Two more things are true of that crate and of no other. Its cardboard base is damp enough to tear when lifted. And the fruit inside tastes mealy and dry even where it is not bruised. Rough handling bruises apples, but it does not make them mealy and it leaves the box dry. Old stock goes mealy, yet every crate on the delivery comes off the same pallet on the same morning. A roof leak would wet the crate below it as well, and the crate below is bone dry. The variety is identical in all five crates, and four of them are fine. The Tuesday crate is the one left on the loading dock overnight because the store room is locked on Mondays. Temperatures on the dock drop below freezing and climb again by morning. Freezing bursts the cells inside the fruit, which is what makes an apple both soft and mealy. Thawing releases that water, and the crate stands in it until the apples are handed out.
q: What is wrong with the Tuesday crate?

sus.who: 🧊 A night on the loading dock
sus.why: the Tuesday crate is left on the dock overnight, where temperatures drop below freezing and climb again by morning
rough handling bruises apples, but it does not make them mealy and it leaves the box dry
every crate on the delivery comes off the same pallet on the same morning
a roof leak would wet the crate below it as well, and the crate below is bone dry
the variety is identical in all five crates, and four of them are fine

ans: The crate freezes and thaws overnight on the loading dock.
proof: “Temperatures on the dock drop below freezing and climb again by morning.”
“Freezing bursts the cells inside the fruit, which is what makes an apple both soft and mealy.”
“Thawing releases that water, and the crate stands in it until the apples are handed out.”
clears: Handling: “it does not make them mealy and it leaves the box dry.”
Old stock: “every crate on the delivery comes off the same pallet on the same morning.”
A leak: “the crate below is bone dry.”
The variety: “the variety is identical in all five crates, and four of them are fine.”
explain: Bruised, mealy and damp look like three faults. Freezing and thawing is one event that produces all three, because burst cells go soft, taste dry, and let their water out. Every other suspect accounts for exactly one column of the table and leaves the other two unexplained.

d.story: Apples from the Tuesday crate bruise within a day of reaching the classrooms. Two more things are true of that crate and of no other. Its cardboard base is damp enough to tear when lifted, and the fruit tastes mealy even where it is not bruised. The Tuesday crate is the one left on the loading dock overnight, because the store room is locked on Mondays. Dock temperatures drop below freezing and climb again by morning, and freezing bursts the cells inside fruit. Burst cells go soft, taste dry, and let their water out into the box. The Tuesday crate is also loaded last, from the back of the cold store, where stock waits longest. Apples held for weeks lose their crispness and bruise under their own weight. A crate that has stood in a cold store carries condensation on its base when it comes out. The roof seam above bay four has dripped since the storm, and the Tuesday crate stands in bay four. Rain fell all Monday night. Every crate is carried by the same two people on the same trolley. All five crates hold the same variety from the same orchard.
d.q: What is wrong with the Tuesday crate? Choose one cause and quote the text.

sus.who: 🧊 A night on the loading dock
sus.why: a night on a dock that freezes and thaws before morning
carried by the same two people on the same trolley
loaded last from the back of the cold store, where stock waits longest
a roof seam over bay four, dripping since the storm
the same variety from the same orchard as the other four

evidence: “The Tuesday crate is the one left on the loading dock overnight, because the store room is locked on Mondays.”
“Dock temperatures drop below freezing and climb again by morning, and freezing bursts the cells inside fruit.”
args.against: “Rain fell all Monday night.”

evidence: “The Tuesday crate is also loaded last, from the back of the cold store, where stock waits longest.”
“Apples held for weeks lose their crispness and bruise under their own weight.”
args.against: “Burst cells go soft, taste dry, and let their water out into the box.”

evidence: “The roof seam above bay four has dripped since the storm, and the Tuesday crate stands in bay four.”
“A crate that has stood in a cold store carries condensation on its base when it comes out.”
args.against: “The fruit tastes mealy even where it is not bruised.”

clears: Rough handling: “Every crate is carried by the same two people on the same trolley.”
The variety: “All five crates hold the same variety from the same orchard.”
d.note: The damp base is the sentence to argue over. Freezing makes it from the inside, the cold store makes it by condensation, the roof seam makes it from above, and the text lets all three stand. Mealiness is where the roof answer runs out, and a good argument says so out loud before someone else does.

title: The Case of the Punctures on the Inside
story: Noor's back tyre goes soft every three or four days, and she has mended it six times. Two details have come up every time and nobody has used them. All six holes are on the inner face of the tube, the side against the wheel. And the cloth rim tape under the tube has slid about a centimetre off true. Thorns and glass pierce a tyre from the outside, and they leave a mark in the tread above the hole. The tread has no cuts anywhere on it. A leaking valve lets air out steadily but leaves no hole to patch, and she has patched six. A worn pump seal would fail to put air in, and the tyre is hard when she sets off. The rim tape exists to cover the spoke ends that poke through the rim bed. Where it has slipped, one spoke end stands proud of the rim with nothing over it. Every time the wheel turns, the tube presses against that end from the inside. That is the only thing touching the tube on the face where all six holes are.
q: What keeps puncturing the tube?

sus.who: 🔩 A spoke end through the slipped tape
sus.why: where the tape has slipped, one spoke end stands proud of the rim with nothing over it
thorns and glass pierce a tyre from the outside, and the tread has no cuts anywhere on it
a leaking valve leaves no hole to patch, and she has patched six
a worn pump seal would fail to put air in, and the tyre is hard when she sets off

ans: A bare spoke end is pressing through where the rim tape slipped.
proof: “Where it has slipped, one spoke end stands proud of the rim with nothing over it.”
“Every time the wheel turns, the tube presses against that end from the inside.”
“That is the only thing touching the tube on the face where all six holes are.”
clears: Thorns: “the tread has no cuts anywhere on it.”
The valve: “a leaking valve lets air out steadily but leaves no hole to patch, and she has patched six.”
The pump: “the tyre is hard when she sets off.”
explain: A slow puncture on its own has four ordinary causes. Add which face the holes are on and where the rim tape sits, and three of the four are gone. The holes are on the inside, so the thing making them is on the inside, and only one thing in the case is.

d.story: Noor's back tyre goes soft every three or four days, and she has mended it six times. Two details come up every time and nobody has used them. Four of the six holes are on the inner face of the tube, and two are on the tread side. The cloth rim tape under the tube has slid about a centimetre off true. Where the tape has slipped, one spoke end stands proud of the rim with nothing over it. Every turn of the wheel presses the tube against that bare end from the inside. Three thorn tips are still embedded in the tread, worn flush and invisible until the tyre is flexed. A thorn held in the rubber pricks the tube again each time the wheel rolls over it. The valve sits in a rim hole whose edge was never filed smooth. Twice the escaping air has been traced to the valve base rather than to any patch. The pump was replaced in September and reads a true sixty on its gauge.
d.q: What keeps puncturing the tube? Pick one and prove it from the story.

sus.who: 🔩 A spoke end through the slipped tape
sus.why: a bare spoke end where the rim tape slipped a centimetre
three thorn tips worn flush into the tread
a valve sitting in a rim hole that was never filed smooth
a pump replaced in September, reading true

evidence: “Where the tape has slipped, one spoke end stands proud of the rim with nothing over it.”
“Every turn of the wheel presses the tube against that bare end from the inside.”
args.against: “Four of the six holes are on the inner face of the tube, and two are on the tread side.”

evidence: “Three thorn tips are still embedded in the tread, worn flush and invisible until the tyre is flexed.”
“A thorn held in the rubber pricks the tube again each time the wheel rolls over it.”
args.against: “The cloth rim tape under the tube has slid about a centimetre off true.”

evidence: “The valve sits in a rim hole whose edge was never filed smooth.”
“Twice the escaping air has been traced to the valve base rather than to any patch.”
args.against: “She has mended it six times.”

clears: The pump: “The pump was replaced in September and reads a true sixty on its gauge.”
d.note: Two holes on the tread side is the whole change from the solve version, and it buys the thorns a case. Four and two is also an argument for two causes at once, which no suspect card offers. A class that gets there has out-reasoned the question, and should be told so.

title: The Case of the Four O'Clock Fish
story: Three complaints about the class tank have been written in the log, on different pages, by different people. The glass grows a green film within three days of being scraped clean. The fish crowd the surface and gulp every afternoon, though they swim low all morning. The thermometer reads nineteen degrees at nine o'clock and twenty-three at four. Overfeeding feeds algae, but it does not warm four degrees of water by teatime. A tired filter would let waste build up slowly and would not keep office hours. Too many fish would crowd the surface in the morning as well as the afternoon. The heater has been unplugged since October, and the plug sits on the shelf beside the tank. The tank was moved in September to the sill under the south window. From half past one the sun falls directly on that glass and stays there until the room is locked. Light is what algae grow on, and sunlight through glass is far stronger than the room lamps. Warm water also holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water does.
q: What is behind all three log entries?

sus.who: ☀️ The afternoon sun on the sill
sus.why: from half past one the sun falls directly on that glass and stays there until the room is locked
overfeeding feeds algae, but it does not warm four degrees of water by teatime
a tired filter would let waste build up slowly and would not keep office hours
too many fish would crowd the surface in the morning as well as the afternoon
the heater has been unplugged since October, and the plug sits on the shelf beside the tank

ans: Afternoon sun through the south window is heating and lighting the tank.
proof: “From half past one the sun falls directly on that glass and stays there until the room is locked.”
“Light is what algae grow on, and sunlight through glass is far stronger than the room lamps.”
“Warm water also holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water does.”
clears: Overfeeding: “it does not warm four degrees of water by teatime.”
The filter: “a tired filter would let waste build up slowly and would not keep office hours.”
Too many fish: “too many fish would crowd the surface in the morning as well as the afternoon.”
The heater: “the heater has been unplugged since October, and the plug sits on the shelf beside the tank.”
explain: Algae, gasping and a rising thermometer were logged as three problems. Sunlight is one cause with three outputs: it feeds the algae, it warms the water, and warm water carries less oxygen, so the fish come up for air exactly when the sun has been on the glass longest.

d.story: Three complaints about the class tank have been written in the log, by different people on different pages. The glass grows a green film within three days of being scraped clean. The fish crowd the surface and gulp every afternoon, though they swim low all morning. The thermometer reads nineteen degrees at nine o'clock and twenty-three at four. The tank was moved in September to the sill under the south window. From half past one the sun falls on that glass and stays there until the room is locked. The lunchtime club feeds the tank again at half past three, on top of the morning feed. Food left to rot takes oxygen out of the water and feeds whatever is growing on the glass. The filter's flow has dropped by half since the sponge was last rinsed in July. Water that is barely turned over lets a warm layer settle at the top and holds waste below it. Six fish were rehomed in October and four remain in a tank built for twelve. The heater has not been in the tank since the summer, and the shelf it sits on is dusty.
d.q: What is behind all three log entries? Choose one cause and quote the text.

sus.who: ☀️ The afternoon sun on the sill
sus.why: a sill under the south window, in sun from half past one
a second feed at half past three, on top of the morning one
a filter whose flow has halved since July
four fish left in a tank built for twelve
a heater out of the water since the summer

evidence: “The tank was moved in September to the sill under the south window.”
“From half past one the sun falls on that glass and stays there until the room is locked.”
args.against: “The filter's flow has dropped by half since the sponge was last rinsed in July.”

evidence: “The lunchtime club feeds the tank again at half past three, on top of the morning feed.”
“Food left to rot takes oxygen out of the water and feeds whatever is growing on the glass.”
args.against: “The thermometer reads nineteen degrees at nine o'clock and twenty-three at four.”

evidence: “The filter's flow has dropped by half since the sponge was last rinsed in July.”
“Water that is barely turned over lets a warm layer settle at the top and holds waste below it.”
args.against: “The fish crowd the surface and gulp every afternoon, though they swim low all morning.”

clears: Too many fish: “Six fish were rehomed in October and four remain in a tank built for twelve.”
The heater: “The heater has not been in the tank since the summer, and the shelf it sits on is dusty.”
d.note: Four degrees by four o'clock is the fact that only the sun reaches cleanly, and the filter answer gets near it with a warm layer that will not mix. The feeding answer cannot touch temperature at all, and it still explains two of the three entries better than either rival. Ask whether two-of-three with a tight fit beats three-of-three with a loose one.

title: The Case of the Rattle on Windy Days
story: Room 12 is unusable whenever the wind gets up, and the caretaker has had three separate reports. There is a hard rattle somewhere near the back wall. A draught crosses the floor strongly enough to lift loose paper off the bottom shelf. And a thin whistle comes and goes at the same times as the rattle. The radiator knocks when it heats, which is first thing on cold mornings, not whenever it is windy. The extractor fan runs on a timer at four o'clock and makes the same sound in still weather. A loose ceiling tile would rattle above head height, and the draught is along the floor. The top window at the back has a catch that no longer engages, which was logged in August and never fixed. An unlatched window is held shut only by its own weight and the frame. Wind pushes it open a few millimetres and lets it fall back, over and over. The gap it opens is narrow, and air forced through a narrow gap whistles. It is also the only opening in the room that the wind can work on.
q: What is making all three noises and the draught?

sus.who: 🪟 The window catch that will not engage
sus.why: the top window at the back has a catch that no longer engages, logged in August and never fixed
the radiator knocks when it heats, which is first thing on cold mornings, not whenever it is windy
the extractor fan runs on a timer at four o'clock and makes the same sound in still weather
a loose ceiling tile would rattle above head height, and the draught is along the floor

ans: The back window is unlatched and the wind is working it.
proof: “Wind pushes it open a few millimetres and lets it fall back, over and over.”
“The gap it opens is narrow, and air forced through a narrow gap whistles.”
“It is also the only opening in the room that the wind can work on.”
clears: The radiator: “not whenever it is windy.”
The fan: “makes the same sound in still weather.”
The ceiling tile: “would rattle above head height, and the draught is along the floor.”
explain: A rattle has several candidates. A rattle plus a floor-level draught plus a whistle, all arriving together with the wind, has one. The unlatched window bangs, lets cold air in and squeezes it through a slot, so three reports are three sides of a single fault.

d.story: Room 12 is unusable whenever the wind gets up, and the caretaker has had three separate reports. There is a hard rattle somewhere near the back wall. A draught crosses the floor strongly enough to lift loose paper off the bottom shelf. And a thin whistle comes and goes at the same times as the rattle. The top window at the back has a catch that no longer engages, logged in August and never fixed. Wind pushes an unlatched window open a few millimetres and lets it fall back, over and over. The extractor cowl on the roof has lost a blade, so the wind spins it whenever it blows. A fan turning backwards pushes cold air down its duct and out at the grille by the skirting. The ceiling tile above the back wall has lifted at one corner, where the void over the cloakroom opens. Air driven through that void comes down behind the cloakroom door and runs along the floor. title: The Case of the Drain by the Gate
story: The drain by the gate floods after every shower, and two other things near it have been reported separately. The path beside the drain is black and slippery for about two metres. And the gutter above that stretch drips steadily even when it has not rained for three days. Blocked drains flood, but a blockage underground does not make a gutter drip in dry weather. Fallen leaves on the path get slippery, yet the caretaker swept and cleared that path on Monday and the slime was back by Wednesday. A cracked downpipe would run down the wall and stain it, and the wall is clean and dry. The gate itself has been replaced this term and sits clear of the drain cover. The gutter above the gate has filled with leaves until it holds water like a trough. Standing water finds the joints and drips for days after the rain stops. When the trough overflows it pours down the same two metres of path, keeping it wet and feeding the slime. The overflow also carries leaf litter straight into the drain below.
q: What is causing the flooding, the slime and the dripping?

a blockage underground does not make a gutter drip in dry weather
the caretaker swept and cleared that path on Monday and the slime was back by Wednesday
a cracked downpipe would run down the wall and stain it, and the wall is clean and dry
the gate itself has been replaced this term and sits clear of the drain cover

ans: The gutter above the gate is packed with leaves and overflowing.
proof: “The gutter above the gate has filled with leaves until it holds water like a trough.”
“Standing water finds the joints and drips for days after the rain stops.”
“The overflow also carries leaf litter straight into the drain below.”
clears: A blockage: “a blockage underground does not make a gutter drip in dry weather.”
Leaves on the path: “the caretaker swept and cleared that path on Monday and the slime was back by Wednesday.”
The downpipe: “the wall is clean and dry.”
The gate: “sits clear of the drain cover.”

title: The Case of the Pumpkin That Lasted Two Weeks
story: Three pumpkins were carved on the same morning from the same box. The one on the office desk collapsed in two days. The porch pumpkin is still standing after a fortnight. A third, also on the office desk, is firm on day ten. Two more things are true only of the collapsed one. Its cut edges carry a fuzzy white bloom, and the inside of its lid has a scorched black ring. A warm room would have taken the third pumpkin too, and the third shares the desk. A bad pumpkin from the box would not produce a scorched ring, which is heat from inside. Thin walls would let it dry out and shrink, and this one went soft and wet instead. The collapsed pumpkin is the only one lit with a real candle. The other two were given battery lights on the same morning. A flame inside a lidded pumpkin scorches the lid directly above it. It also cooks the flesh and drives moisture out of it, and the lid traps that moisture inside. Warm wet flesh in a closed space grows mould within a day.
q: Why did only one pumpkin collapse?

sus.why: the collapsed pumpkin is the only one lit with a real candle, and the other two were given battery lights
a warm room would have taken the third pumpkin too, and the third shares the desk

sus.who: 🧺 A bad pumpkin from the box
sus.why: a bad pumpkin would not produce a scorched ring, which is heat from inside
thin walls would let it dry out and shrink, and this one went soft and wet instead

ans: A burning candle cooked the pumpkin from the inside.
proof: “A flame inside a lidded pumpkin scorches the lid directly above it.”
“It also cooks the flesh and drives moisture out of it, and the lid traps that moisture inside.”
“Warm wet flesh in a closed space grows mould within a day.”
clears: The warm office: “the third shares the desk.”
A bad pumpkin: “a bad pumpkin from the box would not produce a scorched ring, which is heat from inside.”
Thin walls: “this one went soft and wet instead.”
explain: The warm office and the real candle arrived together, so either could be blamed for the collapse. The third pumpkin separates them: same desk, same warmth, no flame, still firm. And only the flame explains the scorched lid and the mould as well, because it supplies both the heat and the trapped steam.

the only one standing above a radiator that runs all day

title: The Case of the Chalky Footprints
story: Grey footprints appear inside the school every morning, and three things about them have been noted and never joined up. They turn up at the east doors and at no door on the west side. They are chalky and pale rather than brown, and they appear on dry days as readily as wet ones. And the dark doormats at the east doors have gone pale across their whole surface. Mud would print brown, and it would need rain, and there has been none since Sunday. The cleaners' new floor product is used on every corridor in the building, including the west side, which is clean. The builders working on the roof come in through the west door and sign in at the west desk. The sandpit sand is yellow, and it is the far side of the field from both doors. A limestone path was laid along the east side at half term. Crushed limestone is white, it powders underfoot, and it does not need to be wet to travel. Shoes carry the dust in, the mats take the first of it, and the floor takes the rest.
q: Where is the grey dust coming from?

sus.why: a limestone path was laid along the east side at half term, and crushed limestone is white and powders underfoot
mud would print brown, and it would need rain, and there has been none since Sunday
the cleaners' new floor product is used on every corridor in the building, including the west side, which is clean
the builders working on the roof come in through the west door and sign in at the west desk
the sandpit sand is yellow, and it is the far side of the field from both doors

ans: Dust from the new limestone path is walking in on shoes.
proof: “A limestone path was laid along the east side at half term.”
“Crushed limestone is white, it powders underfoot, and it does not need to be wet to travel.”
“Shoes carry the dust in, the mats take the first of it, and the floor takes the rest.”
clears: Mud: “mud would print brown, and it would need rain, and there has been none since Sunday.”
The floor product: “used on every corridor in the building, including the west side, which is clean.”
The builders: “come in through the west door and sign in at the west desk.”
The sandpit: “the sandpit sand is yellow, and it is the far side of the field from both doors.”
explain: One door, one colour, one set of ruined mats. Mud explains none of the three, because it is the wrong colour and needs rain. The path explains all three at once: it is on the east side only, it is white, and it gives up powder in dry weather, which is exactly what a pale mat is full of.

title: The Case of the Bus That Ran Late Three Days a Week
story: The 8:05 bus reaches school about seven minutes late, but only on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. Two further facts sit in the driver's log and have never been read beside the first. On those days the bus is already standing room only by stop four. And the whole of the lost time builds up between stop four and stop eight, never before stop four. Roadworks on the main road would slow the bus on all five mornings and on the stretch where they are. The same driver works all five mornings and drives the same route in the same order. The traffic lights at the bridge run on a fixed cycle that does not know what day it is. Wet weather has coincided with Mondays twice this month, and Monday has never been late. The 41 service does not run on Tuesdays, Thursdays or Fridays. Its riders join the 8:05 instead, which is why it fills early on those days. Every passenger on a full bus takes longer to board, and the busy stops are four through eight.
q: Why is the bus late on only three days?

sus.why: the 41 service does not run on Tuesdays, Thursdays or Fridays, and its riders join the 8:05 instead
roadworks on the main road would slow the bus on all five mornings and on the stretch where they are
the same driver works all five mornings and drives the same route in the same order
the traffic lights at the bridge run on a fixed cycle that does not know what day it is
wet weather has coincided with Mondays twice this month, and Monday has never been late

ans: The 41 is cancelled on those days and its riders fill the 8:05.
proof: “The 41 service does not run on Tuesdays, Thursdays or Fridays.”
“Its riders join the 8:05 instead, which is why it fills early on those days.”
“Every passenger on a full bus takes longer to board, and the busy stops are four through eight.”
clears: Roadworks: “would slow the bus on all five mornings and on the stretch where they are.”
The driver: “the same driver works all five mornings and drives the same route in the same order.”
The lights: “run on a fixed cycle that does not know what day it is.”
The weather: “Monday has never been late.”
explain: Lateness on its own points at traffic. Lateness on three named days, a bus already full at stop four, and every lost minute spent in the second half of the route point somewhere else. Only the missing 41 explains the pattern of days and the crowding and the place where the time goes, because the crowding is what spends it.

d.story: The 8:05 bus reaches school about seven minutes late, but only on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. Two further facts sit in the driver's log and have never been read beside the first. a driver whose log shows the same stops in the same order all week
a crossing pattern running on the three mornings the patrol is staffed

“Every passenger on a full bus takes longer to board, and the busy stops are four through eight.”

title: The Case of the Trophy That Blackened on One Side
story: The county cup in the cabinet has gone almost black, and two other details have been noticed without being connected. Only the side facing the back of the cabinet is black, and the front is still bright. And the engraved brass plate screwed to the backing board behind it has dulled to brown over the same weeks. Handling marks silver where fingers grip it, which is the handles and the front, and those are clean. Polish left on the surface would dull it evenly all the way round. Damp in the cabinet would tarnish the two other cups on the glass shelf, and both are bright. The cabinet was refitted in September with a new backing board of untreated oak. Fresh oak gives off faint acidic and sulphurous vapours for months as it seasons. Silver and brass both blacken when sulphur reaches them, and neither needs to be touched. Whatever faces that board gets the vapour first and strongest. The two bright cups stand on the glass shelf a metre away from it.
q: What is blackening the cup?

sus.why: the cabinet was refitted in September with a new backing board of untreated oak
handling marks silver where fingers grip it, which is the handles and the front, and those are clean
polish left on the surface would dull it evenly all the way round
damp would tarnish the two other cups on the glass shelf, and both are bright

ans: Vapour from the untreated oak board is tarnishing the silver.
proof: “Fresh oak gives off faint acidic and sulphurous vapours for months as it seasons.”
“Silver and brass both blacken when sulphur reaches them, and neither needs to be touched.”
“Whatever faces that board gets the vapour first and strongest.”
clears: Handling: “which is the handles and the front, and those are clean.”
Polish: “polish left on the surface would dull it evenly all the way round.”
Damp: “damp in the cabinet would tarnish the two other cups on the glass shelf, and both are bright.”
explain: One blackened face, one dulled brass plate and two bright cups a metre away. Hands and polish and damp each account for tarnish, but none of them account for a direction. The board does. It is new, it is behind the black side, and the only other dull object in the cabinet is the one screwed to it.

“Fresh oak gives off faint acidic and sulphurous vapours for months as it seasons.”

title: The Case of the Turkey That Would Not Brown
story: The turkey came out of the oven wrong in three ways at once. The breast was dry and stringy. The thigh, cut to the bone, was still pink and cool. And the skin was pale and slack after four hours, with no browning anywhere. It also took ninety minutes longer than the recipe allowed. An oven running cold would have left the potatoes on the shelf below underdone, and they came out on time and crisp. A bird too large for the recipe is covered by the recipe, which gives minutes per kilogram. Opening the door often drops the heat briefly, and the door was opened twice. Too much basting liquid would pool in the tin, and the tin was almost dry at the end. The turkey was moved from the freezer to the fridge on the morning of the day before. A bird that size needs three days in a fridge to thaw to the bone. Ice at the centre holds the thigh near zero while the outside cooks and dries. It also melts slowly into steam all through roasting, and a steamy oven cannot brown anything.
q: What went wrong with the turkey?

sus.why: the turkey was moved from the freezer to the fridge on the morning of the day before, and a bird that size needs three days
an oven running cold would have left the potatoes on the shelf below underdone, and they came out on time and crisp
a bird too large for the recipe is covered by the recipe, which gives minutes per kilogram
opening the door often drops the heat briefly, and the door was opened twice
too much basting liquid would pool in the tin, and the tin was almost dry at the end

ans: The turkey went into the oven still frozen at the centre.
proof: “A bird that size needs three days in a fridge to thaw to the bone.”
“Ice at the centre holds the thigh near zero while the outside cooks and dries.”
“It also melts slowly into steam all through roasting, and a steamy oven cannot brown anything.”
clears: A cold oven: “the potatoes on the shelf below” “came out on time and crisp.”
A large bird: “is covered by the recipe, which gives minutes per kilogram.”
The door: “the door was opened twice.”
Basting: “the tin was almost dry at the end.”
explain: Dry breast, raw thigh and pale skin look like three separate failures of cooking. Ice at the centre produces all three. It holds the deep meat cold, it makes the outside wait and overcook, and the water it gives up fills the oven with steam, which is the one thing that stops a skin browning.

title: The Case of the Cupcakes That Rose Too Far
story: Every cupcake in the batch of twenty-four failed, and the failure had three parts. They climbed over the rims of their cases in the first ten minutes. They then sank into craters before the timer went. And they carry a bitter, soapy aftertaste that nobody can place. Opening the oven early makes a cake sink, but it cannot make one rise too high first, and the door stayed shut. Old eggs give a flat, heavy cake that never rises at all. The wrong flour changes the crumb and the colour, and the crumb and colour here are normal. A cold oven would slow everything down, and these were over the rims within ten minutes. The baker doubled the recipe and measured the raising agent with a tablespoon instead of a teaspoon. That is three times the baking powder the doubled recipe asks for. Too much raising agent makes gas faster than the batter can set around it. The structure stretches, runs out of strength and falls, which is what a crater is. Baking powder left over after the rise tastes bitter and faintly of soap.
q: What ruined the cupcakes?

opening the oven early cannot make a cake rise too high first, and the door stayed shut
old eggs give a flat, heavy cake that never rises at all
the wrong flour changes the crumb and the colour, and the crumb and colour here are normal
a cold oven would slow everything down, and these were over the rims within ten minutes

ans: The batch had three times the baking powder it needed.
proof: “Too much raising agent makes gas faster than the batter can set around it.”
“The structure stretches, runs out of strength and falls, which is what a crater is.”
“Baking powder left over after the rise tastes bitter and faintly of soap.”
clears: The oven door: “the door stayed shut.”
Old eggs: “old eggs give a flat, heavy cake that never rises at all.”
The flour: “the crumb and colour here are normal.”
A cold oven: “these were over the rims within ten minutes.”

title: The Case of the Mittens That Came Back Small
story: Six pairs of mittens came out of the lost property wash stiff, thick and two sizes smaller. Two other facts about that load have been mentioned and set aside. Only the wool pairs shrank, and the four acrylic pairs went through the same machine unharmed. And the eleven wool pairs that were hung on the drying rack instead are the size they always were. A hot wash alone would have taken the acrylic pairs too, since acrylic distorts in heat. The detergent was the same tub used on every load this term without complaint. The radiator in the laundry room has been off since the boiler fault in October. Rough handling in a lost property box crushes mittens, and crushing does not thicken wool. The shrunken six went into the tumble dryer on the hot cycle. Wool fibres are covered in tiny scales that hook together when heat and tumbling act at once. Once they hook, they do not let go, and the fabric becomes dense and short. Acrylic has no scales, and wool left to dry still has nothing tumbling it.

a hot wash alone would have taken the acrylic pairs too, since acrylic distorts in heat
the detergent was the same tub used on every load this term without complaint
the radiator in the laundry room has been off since the boiler fault in October
rough handling in a lost property box crushes mittens, and crushing does not thicken wool

“Wool fibres are covered in tiny scales that hook together when heat and tumbling act at once.”
“Acrylic has no scales, and wool left to dry still has nothing tumbling it.”
clears: A hot wash: “would have taken the acrylic pairs too, since acrylic distorts in heat.”
The detergent: “the same tub used on every load this term without complaint.”
The radiator: “has been off since the boiler fault in October.”

title: The Case of the Gingerbread With No Arms
story: The first tray of gingerbread men came out as nine joined blobs with no arms. Two other things about that tray have been reported as separate complaints. The tray came out slick with butter that had run out of the dough. And the second tray, cut from the very same bowl an hour later, held its shape perfectly. Too much butter in the recipe would have ruined the second tray as well, and the bowl was never added to. Tired baking soda makes a flat, dense biscuit, and these spread outward rather than failing to rise. An unlined tray makes biscuits stick, and these lifted off cleanly once cool. An oven set too hot browns the edges hard, and these came out pale. The oven had been on for an hour and the kitchen stood at twenty-six degrees. The first tray was cut and baked straight away from dough that had gone soft and greasy. The second sat in the fridge for forty minutes before it was rolled. Butter that is already half melted cannot hold a shape while the oven melts the rest.
q: Why did only the first tray spread?

sus.why: the oven had been on for an hour and the kitchen stood at twenty-six degrees, and the first tray was baked straight away
too much butter in the recipe would have ruined the second tray as well, and the bowl was never added to
tired baking soda makes a flat, dense biscuit, and these spread outward rather than failing to rise
an unlined tray makes biscuits stick, and these lifted off cleanly once cool
an oven set too hot browns the edges hard, and these came out pale

ans: The first tray was baked from dough already warm and soft.
proof: “The oven had been on for an hour and the kitchen stood at twenty-six degrees.”
“The second sat in the fridge for forty minutes before it was rolled.”
“Butter that is already half melted cannot hold a shape while the oven melts the rest.”
clears: Too much butter: “the bowl was never added to.”
Baking soda: “these spread outward rather than failing to rise.”
The tray: “these lifted off cleanly once cool.”
A hot oven: “these came out pale.”
explain: Same bowl, same oven, same baker, two different results. That rules out everything in the recipe at a stroke, because a recipe fault would have to show in both trays. What differs is forty minutes in the fridge, and warm butter explains the spreading, the greasy tray and the arms that vanished.

title: The Case of the Lights That Failed in the Rain
story: The display lights in the front window go dead whenever it rains and work again once the weather clears. Two more facts have been reported by different people on different days. The whole circuit trips at the fuse box at the same moment the lights go out. And the brass holder of the bulb closest to the window frame is crusted green. A blown bulb takes out its own lamp and sometimes the string, but it does not trip a circuit. A loose plug at the socket would cut the lights in dry weather as often as wet. The timer switch has been replaced twice and the fault followed the lights, not the timer. A shortage of power in the building would darken the corridor lights as well, and they stay on. The window frame above that holder has a crack in its seal that lets rain run inside. Water bridging the two contacts in a holder carries current where it should not go. That is a fault to earth, which is the one thing that makes a modern fuse box trip. Standing water on brass also corrodes it green, slowly and only where the water sits.
q: Why do the lights die in the rain?

a blown bulb takes out its own lamp and sometimes the string, but it does not trip a circuit
a loose plug at the socket would cut the lights in dry weather as often as wet
the timer switch has been replaced twice and the fault followed the lights, not the timer
a shortage of power in the building would darken the corridor lights as well, and they stay on

ans: Rain through a cracked seal is reaching one bulb holder.
proof: “Water bridging the two contacts in a holder carries current where it should not go.”
“That is a fault to earth, which is the one thing that makes a modern fuse box trip.”
“Standing water on brass also corrodes it green, slowly and only where the water sits.”
clears: A blown bulb: “it does not trip a circuit.”
A loose plug: “would cut the lights in dry weather as often as wet.”
The timer: “the fault followed the lights, not the timer.”
A power shortage: “they stay on.”
explain: Three facts, each dismissed alone: dead in the rain, a tripping fuse box, a green holder. Water in one holder is the single cause that produces all three, and the green crust is the record of where it has been sitting every wet week since the seal cracked.

title: The Case of the Clock That Lost Time When It Was Warm
story: The pendulum clock in the entrance hall loses about four minutes a day, and the loss is not steady. Two other observations sit in the caretaker's book without comment. The clock keeps near perfect time through the cold months and slips badly in warm weather. And the left side of its wooden case, the side nearest the wall, is noticeably warm by the afternoon. A worn mainspring weakens as it unwinds, which would lose time late in the day every day of the year. Dust in the gears adds friction that does not care what month it is. A clock hanging off level stops or runs wild, and this one has run steadily for thirty years. A weak chime spring affects the striking, not the going train. The old radiator in the hall was replaced in April with a much larger one. The new radiator stands directly against the wall behind the clock. A pendulum's swing is timed by its length, and a longer pendulum swings more slowly. Brass expands when it is heated, so a warm brass rod hangs its weight lower than a cold one.
q: Why does the clock lose time?

sus.why: the new radiator stands directly against the wall behind the clock, and brass expands when it is heated
a worn mainspring would lose time late in the day every day of the year
dust in the gears adds friction that does not care what month it is
a clock hanging off level stops or runs wild, and this one has run steadily for thirty years
a weak chime spring affects the striking, not the going train

ans: Heat from the new radiator is lengthening the brass pendulum.
proof: “A pendulum's swing is timed by its length, and a longer pendulum swings more slowly.”
“Brass expands when it is heated, so a warm brass rod hangs its weight lower than a cold one.”
“The new radiator stands directly against the wall behind the clock.”
clears: The mainspring: “would lose time late in the day every day of the year.”
Dust: “adds friction that does not care what month it is.”
Off level: “this one has run steadily for thirty years.”
The chime spring: “affects the striking, not the going train.”
explain: Losing time has four mechanical explanations and all of them are year round. The clock only loses in warm weather, its case is warm on one side, and a bigger radiator went in behind it in April. Heat is upstream of all three, and the physics is ordinary: warm brass is longer, a longer pendulum is slower.

title: The Case of the Stripes in the Roof Snow
story: Two bare stripes have melted through the snow on the school roof while the rest of it lies thick. Two other facts belong with them and have been treated as separate problems. Long icicles hang from the gutter directly below those two stripes and nowhere else. And rooms fourteen and fifteen, which sit under them, are the two coldest rooms in the building. Sun would clear the whole south slope rather than two stripes a metre wide. The boiler flue comes out through the far end of the roof, thirty metres from either stripe. A hot water pipe in the roof space would run the length of the building and melt a line along it. The snow fell evenly and settled to the same depth everywhere on the first night. The loft insulation was lifted between two pairs of rafters in October and never put back. Warm room air now reaches the roof slates directly in those two gaps. Heat that escapes through a roof melts the snow sitting on it and leaves the rest alone. The water runs down to the cold gutter beyond the warm patch and freezes there.

sus.why: the loft insulation was lifted between two pairs of rafters in October and never put back
sun would clear the whole south slope rather than two stripes a metre wide
the boiler flue comes out through the far end of the roof, thirty metres from either stripe
a hot water pipe in the roof space would run the length of the building and melt a line along it
the snow fell evenly and settled to the same depth everywhere on the first night

ans: Heat is escaping through two gaps in the loft insulation.
proof: “Warm room air now reaches the roof slates directly in those two gaps.”
“Heat that escapes through a roof melts the snow sitting on it and leaves the rest alone.”
“The water runs down to the cold gutter beyond the warm patch and freezes there.”
clears: The sun: “would clear the whole south slope rather than two stripes a metre wide.”
The flue: “comes out through the far end of the roof, thirty metres from either stripe.”
A hot pipe: “would run the length of the building and melt a line along it.”
Uneven snowfall: “the snow fell evenly and settled to the same depth everywhere on the first night.”

title: The Case of the Feeder With No Husks

Wind strong enough to empty a feeder would also take the light plastic lid, which is still in place, though it has been turned a quarter round. An animal that eats seed whole leaves no husks anywhere. The grease on the pole was put there in November and has been scratched through since. Something with claws has been climbing a pole it was meant to slide down. Something with paws has been lifting a lid that birds cannot work.
q: What is emptying the feeder?
