birds crack a seed, swallow the kernel and drop the husk, so a busy feeder always litters
a spill would scatter whole seed on the grass, and the grass underneath is bare
the caretaker fills the feeder on Monday mornings only and has not changed that
wind strong enough to empty a feeder would also take the light plastic lid, which is still in place

ans: An animal with claws is climbing the pole and opening the lid.
proof: “An animal that eats seed whole leaves no husks anywhere.”
“The grease on the pole was put there in November and has been scratched through since.”
“Something with paws has been lifting a lid that birds cannot work.”
clears: Birds: “so a busy feeder always litters.”
A spill: “the grass underneath is bare.”
The caretaker: “fills the feeder on Monday mornings only and has not changed that.”
The wind: “which is still in place, though it has been turned a quarter round.”
explain: An empty feeder on its own says nothing. An empty feeder with no husks says the eater swallows the shell. Scratches through fresh grease say it climbs, and a lid turned a quarter round says it has paws. Three details, and only one kind of visitor fits all of them.

d.story: The bird feeder by the field empties every night, and two further details have been noticed without being joined. There are no sunflower husks on the ground beneath it, though the grass below the old feeder was always carpeted with them. And the greased pole has four sets of long scratch lines running up it. The grease on the pole was put there in November and has been scratched through since. Something with claws has been climbing a pole it was meant to slide down, and lifting a lid that birds cannot work. The caretaker switched in November to a hulled sunflower mix with the husks already taken off. A bird eating hulled seed has nothing to drop, so a busy feeder leaves a clean floor. The feeder hangs on the exposed field corner, where the wind funnels between the hall and the fence. Its lid has been found turned a quarter round on four of the last five mornings. A lid turned off its catch lets seed pour out of the top on its own. The chain it hangs by swings against the pole in any wind and drags its links down the grease. The ground beneath is bare earth with no whole seed anywhere on it. The caretaker fills it on Monday mornings and has not been near it since.
d.q: What is emptying the feeder? Choose one and quote the story.

sus.why: claws through the grease and a lid that birds cannot work
a hulled mix, switched in November, that leaves nothing to drop
bare earth beneath with no whole seed anywhere on it
a Monday fill and nobody near it since
an exposed corner and a lid found turned four mornings in five

evidence: “The grease on the pole was put there in November and has been scratched through since.”
“Something with claws has been climbing a pole it was meant to slide down, and lifting a lid that birds cannot work.”
args.against: “The chain it hangs by swings against the pole in any wind and drags its links down the grease.”

evidence: “The caretaker switched in November to a hulled sunflower mix with the husks already taken off.”
“A bird eating hulled seed has nothing to drop, so a busy feeder leaves a clean floor.”
args.against: “The bird feeder by the field empties every night”

evidence: “The feeder hangs on the exposed field corner, where the wind funnels between the hall and the fence.”
“Its lid has been found turned a quarter round on four of the last five mornings.”
args.against: “The ground beneath is bare earth with no whole seed anywhere on it.”

clears: A spill: “The ground beneath is bare earth with no whole seed anywhere on it.”
The caretaker: “The caretaker fills it on Monday mornings and has not been near it since.”
d.note: The missing husks used to prove it was not birds. A hulled mix explains them away in one sentence, and November gives the chain a reason to scratch grease. Note that the wind answer and the bird answer both leave seed somewhere, and the ground is bare: that is the sentence to make a class account for.

title: The Case of the Watery Cocoa
story: The cocoa from the machine in the staff room is barely warm, and two other complaints have been pinned to the wall beside it. It tastes thin and pale, as if it had been made with half the powder. And the drip tray underneath, which used to be emptied on Fridays, now fills by Wednesday. Old powder tastes flat but it does not make a drink cooler. A failing heater would give a cold drink at full strength, not a weak one. Dirty cups would change nothing about the volume that comes out. A blocked powder chute would thicken what remains in the cup, not thin it. The water valve was replaced in January with one from a different model. It passes almost twice the water per cup that the old one did. The same scoop of powder now has to colour and flavour twice as much liquid. The heater warms what passes through it at a fixed rate, so twice the water comes out cooler. And a cup sized for the old dose overflows into the tray every time.
q: What is wrong with the machine?

sus.why: the water valve was replaced in January with one that passes almost twice the water per cup
old powder tastes flat but it does not make a drink cooler
a failing heater would give a cold drink at full strength, not a weak one
dirty cups would change nothing about the volume that comes out
a blocked powder chute would thicken what remains in the cup, not thin it

ans: The new valve is sending almost twice the water into every cup.
proof: “The same scoop of powder now has to colour and flavour twice as much liquid.”
“The heater warms what passes through it at a fixed rate, so twice the water comes out cooler.”
“And a cup sized for the old dose overflows into the tray every time.”
clears: Old powder: “it does not make a drink cooler.”
The heater: “would give a cold drink at full strength, not a weak one.”
Dirty cups: “would change nothing about the volume that comes out.”
The chute: “would thicken what remains in the cup, not thin it.”
explain: Weak, cool and overflowing were posted as three complaints by three people. They are one number changed. Doubling the water dilutes the powder, outruns the heater and fills a cup that was never sized for it, so the tray fills two days early as well.

d.story: The cocoa from the machine in the staff room is barely warm, and two other complaints are pinned to the wall beside it. It tastes thin and pale, as if it had been made with half the powder. And the drip tray underneath, which used to be emptied on Fridays, now fills by Wednesday. The water valve was replaced in January with one from a different model. It passes almost twice the water per cup that the old one did. A cup sized for the old dose overflows into the tray every time. The heating element was descaled in January and refitted with a thermostat from the spares drawer. An element running below its setting leaves half the powder undissolved at the bottom of the cup. The powder chute has furred with damp since January and no longer clears in one go. A jammed chute holds the dosing arm down, and the arm holds the water valve open while it tries again. Heat added at a fixed rate is spread thinner the more water a cup is given. The powder tub was opened on Monday and its date runs to next August. The cups come sealed in sleeves of fifty and are never handled before use.
d.q: Why is the cocoa thin and cool? Pick one cause and prove it from the text.

sus.why: a January valve passing almost twice the water per cup
a tub opened on Monday, dated to next August
an element refitted with a thermostat from the spares drawer
cups sealed in sleeves of fifty, never handled before use
a furred chute that jams the dosing arm down

evidence: “The water valve was replaced in January with one from a different model.”
“It passes almost twice the water per cup that the old one did.”
args.against: “An element running below its setting leaves half the powder undissolved at the bottom of the cup.”

evidence: “The heating element was descaled in January and refitted with a thermostat from the spares drawer.”
“An element running below its setting leaves half the powder undissolved at the bottom of the cup.”
args.against: “And the drip tray underneath, which used to be emptied on Fridays, now fills by Wednesday.”

evidence: “The powder chute has furred with damp since January and no longer clears in one go.”
“A jammed chute holds the dosing arm down, and the arm holds the water valve open while it tries again.”
args.against: “It passes almost twice the water per cup that the old one did.”

clears: Old powder: “The powder tub was opened on Monday and its date runs to next August.”
Dirty cups: “The cups come sealed in sleeves of fifty and are never handled before use.”
d.note: Everything in this machine was worked on in January, which is how real faults arrive and why one symptom rarely picks one cause. The chute answer is the one worth chasing: it reaches all three complaints by making the valve misbehave, so it is both a rival to the valve and an explanation of it.

title: The Case of the Cards in the Postbox
story: Every card that spent a night in the class postbox came out marked, and three things were wrong with them at once. The ink had feathered and smudged on the envelopes. The envelopes themselves had gone wavy along the bottom edge. And the inside of the box's metal base is freckled with new rust. Cards handed over by hand on the same morning, written with the same pens, are crisp and clean. Cheap glue on a flap softens at the seal, and these flaps are firm and the marks are everywhere. A spilled drink would soak some cards and miss others, and all nineteen are marked alike. Handling smudges wet ink in streaks, and this ink has spread in soft haloes. The box stands on the cold windowsill with the window left on its latch all night. Warm room air meeting cold metal leaves water on every inside surface it touches. Damp paper swells where it takes up water, which is why an edge goes wavy. Ink spreads into damp fibre on its own, with nothing rubbing it, and bare steel rusts the same night.
q: What spoiled the cards?

sus.why: warm room air meeting cold metal leaves water on every inside surface it touches
cards handed over by hand on the same morning, written with the same pens, are crisp and clean
cheap glue on a flap softens at the seal, and these flaps are firm and the marks are everywhere
a spilled drink would soak some cards and miss others, and all nineteen are marked alike
handling smudges wet ink in streaks, and this ink has spread in soft haloes

ans: Condensation formed inside the cold metal box overnight.
proof: “The box stands on the cold windowsill with the window left on its latch all night.”
“Damp paper swells where it takes up water, which is why an edge goes wavy.”
“Ink spreads into damp fibre on its own, with nothing rubbing it, and bare steel rusts the same night.”
clears: The pens: “written with the same pens, are crisp and clean.”
The glue: “these flaps are firm and the marks are everywhere.”
A drink: “all nineteen are marked alike.”
Handling: “this ink has spread in soft haloes.”
explain: Smudged ink alone would send you after the pens. Smudged ink with wavy edges and fresh rust sends you after water, and the only water in the case is the water the air puts there. A card in a hand all morning is the control, and it came out clean.

d.story: Every card that spent a night in the class postbox came out marked, and three things were wrong with them at once. The ink had feathered and smudged on the envelopes. The envelopes themselves had gone wavy along the bottom edge. And the inside of the box's metal base is freckled with new rust. The box stands on the cold windowsill with the window left on its latch all night. Warm room air meeting cold metal leaves water on every inside surface it touches. The nineteen boxed cards were all written at the back table with the new roller pens. The hand-delivered cards were written at the front table with the old ballpoints. Roller ink is water-based and spreads into any fibre that is even slightly damp. A bottle of squash went over on the shelf above the box on Thursday evening. It ran down the wall and in through the posting slot, which is the only opening the box has. Liquid entering a sealed metal box pools in the base and reaches every card standing in it. Both flaps and seals are firm, and no glue line on any of the nineteen has lifted. Each card was carried in by its writer and dropped straight through the slot.
d.q: What marked the cards? Choose one cause and quote the story.

sus.why: a cold metal box on a sill with the window latched open all night
roller pens at the back table, ballpoints at the front
flaps and seals firm, with no glue line lifted
a squash bottle over on the shelf above, on Thursday evening
each card carried in by its writer and dropped straight through

evidence: “The box stands on the cold windowsill with the window left on its latch all night.”
“Warm room air meeting cold metal leaves water on every inside surface it touches.”
args.against: “A bottle of squash went over on the shelf above the box on Thursday evening.”

evidence: “The nineteen boxed cards were all written at the back table with the new roller pens.”
“Roller ink is water-based and spreads into any fibre that is even slightly damp.”
args.against: “And the inside of the box's metal base is freckled with new rust.”

evidence: “A bottle of squash went over on the shelf above the box on Thursday evening.”
“It ran down the wall and in through the posting slot, which is the only opening the box has.”
args.against: “Every card that spent a night in the class postbox came out marked”

clears: Cheap glue: “Both flaps and seals are firm, and no glue line on any of the nineteen has lifted.”
Handling: “Each card was carried in by its writer and dropped straight through the slot.”
d.note: The pens answer is the trap worth setting, because it is true and insufficient at the same time. Water-based ink explains the feathering perfectly and explains the rust not at all, so a group that chooses it has to argue that two causes are at work. That is a legitimate answer, and it should be marked as one.

title: The Case of the Volcano That Barely Erupted
story: The model volcano at the science fair gave a slow dribble instead of an eruption, and two more things were odd about it. The foam that did come out was pink rather than the deep red of every rehearsal. And a third of the liquid was still sitting in the bottle when the crowd moved on. Old bicarbonate fizzes weakly, but the same tub ran the rehearsal an hour earlier at full force. A narrow neck slows the foam without weakening the fizz, and the bottle was never changed. A cold room slows a reaction a little, and the hall was the same temperature as the classroom. Too little bicarbonate would leave vinegar behind, and the scoop was measured twice. The vinegar bottle was found three centimetres fuller than it was left after the rehearsal. Somebody topped it up from the tap to make it look untouched. Diluted vinegar carries less acid, so it makes less gas and makes it more slowly. The same dilution thins the red colouring already mixed into it. And a reaction that runs out of acid before it runs out of liquid leaves liquid behind.
q: Why did the volcano fail?

sus.why: the vinegar bottle was found three centimetres fuller than it was left after the rehearsal
the same tub ran the rehearsal an hour earlier at full force
a narrow neck slows the foam without weakening the fizz, and the bottle was never changed
a cold room slows a reaction a little, and the hall was the same temperature as the classroom
too little bicarbonate would leave vinegar behind, and the scoop was measured twice

ans: The vinegar had been watered down before the show.
proof: “Somebody topped it up from the tap to make it look untouched.”
“Diluted vinegar carries less acid, so it makes less gas and makes it more slowly.”
“The same dilution thins the red colouring already mixed into it.”
clears: Old bicarbonate: “the same tub ran the rehearsal an hour earlier at full force.”
The neck: “the bottle was never changed.”
The room: “the hall was the same temperature as the classroom.”
The scoop: “the scoop was measured twice.”
explain: A weak eruption has four innocent explanations and none of them turns red into pink. Water does. It is also the only one that explains why liquid was left in the bottle, because a watered acid runs out of strength long before it runs out of volume.

d.story: The model volcano at the science fair gave a slow dribble instead of an eruption, and two more things were odd about it. The foam that did come out was pink rather than the deep red of every rehearsal. And a third of the liquid was still sitting in the bottle when the crowd moved on. The vinegar bottle was found three centimetres fuller than it was left after the rehearsal. Somebody topped it up from the tap to make it look untouched. Diluted vinegar carries less acid, so it makes less gas and thins the red colouring mixed into it. The tub carried to the hall was a second one, taken from the back of the cupboard and caked solid. The rehearsal an hour earlier was run from the open tub left on the bench. Caked bicarbonate dissolves slowly, so much of it never meets the acid at all. The scoop was levelled off twice over, and half of it was later found stuck inside the paper funnel. A reaction that runs out of one ingredient before the other leaves the other sitting in the bottle. The same bottle and the same neck were used at the rehearsal and at the fair. The hall thermometer and the classroom thermometer both read nineteen degrees all afternoon.
d.q: Why did the volcano barely erupt? Pick one cause and prove it.

sus.why: a vinegar bottle three centimetres fuller than it was left
a second tub from the back of the cupboard, caked solid
the same bottle and the same neck as the rehearsal
two thermometers both reading nineteen degrees all afternoon
half a scoop found stuck inside the paper funnel

evidence: “The vinegar bottle was found three centimetres fuller than it was left after the rehearsal.”
“Somebody topped it up from the tap to make it look untouched.”
args.against: “The scoop was levelled off twice over, and half of it was later found stuck inside the paper funnel.”

evidence: “The tub carried to the hall was a second one, taken from the back of the cupboard and caked solid.”
“Caked bicarbonate dissolves slowly, so much of it never meets the acid at all.”
args.against: “The foam that did come out was pink rather than the deep red of every rehearsal.”

evidence: “The scoop was levelled off twice over, and half of it was later found stuck inside the paper funnel.”
“A reaction that runs out of one ingredient before the other leaves the other sitting in the bottle.”
args.against: “Diluted vinegar carries less acid, so it makes less gas and thins the red colouring mixed into it.”

clears: A narrow neck: “The same bottle and the same neck were used at the rehearsal and at the fair.”
A cold room: “The hall thermometer and the classroom thermometer both read nineteen degrees all afternoon.”
d.note: The pink foam is the only fact that separates these three, because a short measure of bicarbonate cannot dilute a colour and a caked tub cannot either. Watch for the group that says the leftover liquid proves too little bicarbonate, and ask them what the colour costs that answer.

title: The Case of the Crowns That Curled
story: Half the paper crowns made in Tuesday's lesson had curled backwards into tubes within the hour. Two other facts were mentioned and set aside at the time. Every curled crown is one of the glued ones, and the stapled crowns are still flat. And each curled crown has turned slightly see-through in a band along the glued seam. The radiator heats the whole room, and both kinds of crown sat on the same two tables. Thin card would curl whichever way it was held, and the curl here is always toward the glued face. The paint was used on all twenty-four crowns, and twelve of them are perfect. Rough handling creases card, and there is not a crease on any of them. The glue is the water-based stick from the art cupboard, spread along one face only. Paper swells where water soaks in and shrinks again as that water leaves. One face of the card has been wetted and the other has not. A sheet that shrinks on one side and not the other has nowhere to go but round.
q: Why did half the crowns curl?

sus.why: the glue is the water-based stick from the art cupboard, spread along one face only
the radiator heats the whole room, and both kinds of crown sat on the same two tables
thin card would curl whichever way it was held, and the curl here is always toward the glued face
the paint was used on all twenty-four crowns, and twelve of them are perfect
rough handling creases card, and there is not a crease on any of them

ans: Wet glue on one face shrank that side of the card as it dried.
proof: “Paper swells where water soaks in and shrinks again as that water leaves.”
“One face of the card has been wetted and the other has not.”
“A sheet that shrinks on one side and not the other has nowhere to go but round.”
clears: The radiator: “both kinds of crown sat on the same two tables.”
Thin card: “the curl here is always toward the glued face.”
The paint: “twelve of them are perfect.”
Handling: “there is not a crease on any of them.”
explain: The stapled twelve are a control nobody set up on purpose. Same card, same paint, same radiator, no curl. What is left is the water in the glue, and it also explains the direction of the curl and the translucent band, because both are records of where the paper got wet.

d.story: Half the paper crowns made in Tuesday's lesson had curled backwards into tubes within the hour. Two other facts were mentioned and set aside at the time. Every curled crown is one of the glued ones, and the stapled crowns are still flat. And each curled crown has turned slightly see-through in a band along the glued seam. The glue is the water-based stick from the art cupboard, spread along one face only. Paper swells where water soaks in and shrinks again as that water leaves. A sheet that shrinks on one side and not the other has nowhere to go but round. The glued crowns were laid along the windowsill over the radiator to dry. The stapled ones went straight into the drying tray on the far side of the room. Heat drives water out of one face far faster than it leaves the other. The twelve glued crowns were the painted ones, brushed on their inside face only. The stapled twelve were left bare because the paint ran out at the halfway point. Every crown was cut from the same sheet of three hundred gram card. Not one of the twenty-four has a crease, a fold line or a torn corner.
d.q: Why did half the crowns curl? Choose one cause and quote the text.

sus.why: a water-based stick spread along one face only
the glued twelve laid over the radiator, the stapled twelve across the room
all twenty-four cut from the same sheet of three hundred gram card
paint brushed on the inside face of the glued twelve alone
not one crease, fold line or torn corner on any of them

evidence: “The glue is the water-based stick from the art cupboard, spread along one face only.”
“Paper swells where water soaks in and shrinks again as that water leaves.”
args.against: “The twelve glued crowns were the painted ones, brushed on their inside face only.”

evidence: “The glued crowns were laid along the windowsill over the radiator to dry.”
“The stapled ones went straight into the drying tray on the far side of the room.”
args.against: “And each curled crown has turned slightly see-through in a band along the glued seam.”

evidence: “The twelve glued crowns were the painted ones, brushed on their inside face only.”
“The stapled twelve were left bare because the paint ran out at the halfway point.”
args.against: “A sheet that shrinks on one side and not the other has nowhere to go but round.”

clears: Thin card: “Every crown was cut from the same sheet of three hundred gram card.”
Rough handling: “Not one of the twenty-four has a crease, a fold line or a torn corner.”
d.note: Glued, painted and warmed are now the same twelve crowns, which is exactly the confound a real experiment runs into. Nothing in the text separates them, and the honest answer says so and names the test: glue twelve more, paint none of them, dry them in the tray.

title: The Case of the Piano That Would Not Stay in Tune
story: The hall piano is noticeably flat three weeks after every tuning, and two other facts have never been put beside that one. The drop is worst in the treble and barely noticeable in the bass. And two hairline cracks have opened along the grain of the soundboard since September. The tuner has worked on it for eleven years and his other pianos hold their pitch for a year. Hard playing knocks individual strings out, which gives sour notes rather than a whole register sinking together. The move from the old hall happened in July, and the piano was flat again in October, January and March. A loose tuning pin lets one string slip, and every treble string has gone the same way. The hall is heated all day and the humidity gauge on the wall has read between twenty and twenty-six percent all winter. Wood gives up its moisture to dry air and shrinks as it goes. A shrinking soundboard flattens, which lets the strings above it slacken. Dry wood also splits along its grain, and the treble strings are the shortest and the quickest to show a change.
q: Why does the piano go flat?

sus.why: the humidity gauge on the wall has read between twenty and twenty-six percent all winter
the tuner has worked on it for eleven years and his other pianos hold their pitch for a year
hard playing knocks individual strings out, which gives sour notes rather than a whole register sinking together

sus.who: 🚚 The move from the old hall
sus.why: the move happened in July, and the piano was flat again in October, January and March
a loose tuning pin lets one string slip, and every treble string has gone the same way

ans: Dry air in the heated hall is shrinking the soundboard.
proof: “Wood gives up its moisture to dry air and shrinks as it goes.”
“A shrinking soundboard flattens, which lets the strings above it slacken.”
“Dry wood also splits along its grain, and the treble strings are the shortest and the quickest to show a change.”
clears: The tuner: “his other pianos hold their pitch for a year.”
Hard playing: “which gives sour notes rather than a whole register sinking together.”
The move: “the piano was flat again in October, January and March.”
A loose pin: “every treble string has gone the same way.”
explain: Going flat, going flat unevenly, and splitting along the grain are three faces of one thing leaving the instrument: water. Blame the tuner and you still owe an explanation for the cracks. Dry air owes nothing, because shrinking wood both slackens strings and splits.

d.story: The hall piano is noticeably flat three weeks after every tuning, and two other facts have never been put beside that one. The drop is worst in the treble and barely noticeable in the bass. And two hairline cracks have opened along the grain of the soundboard since September. The hall is heated all day and the humidity gauge on the wall has read between twenty and twenty-six percent all winter. Wood gives up its moisture to dry air and shrinks as it goes, and dry wood splits along its grain. A shrinking soundboard flattens, which lets the strings above it slacken. The piano was moved here in July from the old hall, which was unheated and read sixty percent. An instrument that spent forty years at one humidity has been losing water ever since. The pinblock was found dry and shrunken when the tuner opened it in September. Every treble pin now turns under a finger, and a pin that turns lets its string slip. Treble strings are the shortest and the quickest to show any change at all. The tuner has worked on this piano for eleven years and his other pianos hold a year. The lid has been locked since September and only two staff have the key.
d.q: Why will the piano not hold its tuning? Pick one cause and prove it.

sus.why: a heated hall reading twenty to twenty-six percent all winter
eleven years on this piano, and other pianos that hold a year
a locked lid since September, with two keys in the building

sus.who: 🚚 The move from the old hall
sus.why: a July move from an unheated hall that read sixty percent
a dry, shrunken pinblock with every treble pin turning

evidence: “The hall is heated all day and the humidity gauge on the wall has read between twenty and twenty-six percent all winter.”
“Wood gives up its moisture to dry air and shrinks as it goes, and dry wood splits along its grain.”
args.against: “An instrument that spent forty years at one humidity has been losing water ever since.”

evidence: “The piano was moved here in July from the old hall, which was unheated and read sixty percent.”
“An instrument that spent forty years at one humidity has been losing water ever since.”
args.against: “A shrinking soundboard flattens, which lets the strings above it slacken.”

evidence: “The pinblock was found dry and shrunken when the tuner opened it in September.”
“Every treble pin now turns under a finger, and a pin that turns lets its string slip.”
args.against: “And two hairline cracks have opened along the grain of the soundboard since September.”

clears: The tuner: “The tuner has worked on this piano for eleven years and his other pianos hold a year.”
Hard playing: “The lid has been locked since September and only two staff have the key.”
d.note: The dry hall, the move and the pinblock are one physical story told from three places, and a class that notices that has understood the case better than one that picks a winner. Push them to say which is the cause and which are its effects, and whether the question even has a single right level.

title: The Case of the Kite That Dived Left
story: The kite climbs, hangs for a second and then swings hard to the left and hits the ground. It has done this eleven times in a row. Two other things are true and were taken for coincidence. The paper over the left half is a shade darker than the paper over the right. And the kite flew straight for two hours on Saturday, before it was left out on the grass overnight. A badly tied bridle pulls a kite over, but the bridle has not been retied since Saturday. Gusty wind throws a kite in whatever direction it happens to come from, and this kite goes left in a steady breeze. A tail that is too short makes a kite swing from side to side rather than always one way. A torn covering spills air through the hole, and the paper is whole on both sides. Dew soaked the lower half of the kite as it lay on the grass. Damp paper and a damp wooden spar both hold water, and water has weight. The left side is now heavier than the right, and a heavier side drops. Darker paper is wetter paper, and it is wetter because that is the side that lay down.
q: Why does the kite always dive left?

sus.why: dew soaked the lower half of the kite as it lay on the grass, and water has weight
a badly tied bridle pulls a kite over, but the bridle has not been retied since Saturday
gusty wind throws a kite in whatever direction it happens to come from, and this kite goes left in a steady breeze
a tail that is too short makes a kite swing from side to side rather than always one way
a torn covering spills air through the hole, and the paper is whole on both sides

ans: The left half soaked up dew overnight and is now heavier.
proof: “Dew soaked the lower half of the kite as it lay on the grass.”
“The left side is now heavier than the right, and a heavier side drops.”
“Darker paper is wetter paper, and it is wetter because that is the side that lay down.”
clears: The bridle: “the bridle has not been retied since Saturday.”
The wind: “this kite goes left in a steady breeze.”
The tail: “makes a kite swing from side to side rather than always one way.”
A tear: “the paper is whole on both sides.”
explain: Always the same direction rules out the wind and the tail, because neither has a favourite side. Nothing was altered on the kite, which rules out the bridle. What changed was a night on wet grass, and that single change left its own evidence in the colour of the paper.

d.story: The kite climbs, hangs for a second and then swings hard to the left and hits the ground. It has done this eleven times in a row. Two other things are true and were taken for coincidence. The paper over the left half is a shade darker than the paper over the right. And the kite flew straight for two hours on Saturday, before it was left out on the grass overnight. Dew soaked the lower half of the kite as it lay on the grass. Damp paper and a damp wooden spar both hold water, and water has weight. The bridle knot slipped when the kite was dragged in off the grass on Sunday morning. Its left leg now measures two centimetres shorter than its right, which tips the whole frame that way. The tail lost half its length on Saturday evening and nobody replaced it. What is left of it is knotted to the left corner of the kite rather than to the centre. A tail pulling from one corner drags that corner down every time the kite loses speed. The breeze has held steady from the west at nine miles an hour all week. Both sides of the covering are intact, with no tear, hole or split seam anywhere.
d.q: Why does the kite dive left? Choose one cause and quote the story.

sus.why: a left half left lying on wet grass and still darker than the right
a bridle knot that slipped, leaving the left leg two centimetres short
a steady westerly at nine miles an hour all week
half a tail, knotted to the left corner instead of the centre
a covering intact on both sides, with no tear or split seam

evidence: “Dew soaked the lower half of the kite as it lay on the grass.”
“Damp paper and a damp wooden spar both hold water, and water has weight.”
args.against: “Its left leg now measures two centimetres shorter than its right, which tips the whole frame that way.”

evidence: “The bridle knot slipped when the kite was dragged in off the grass on Sunday morning.”
“Its left leg now measures two centimetres shorter than its right, which tips the whole frame that way.”
args.against: “The paper over the left half is a shade darker than the paper over the right.”

evidence: “The tail lost half its length on Saturday evening and nobody replaced it.”
“What is left of it is knotted to the left corner of the kite rather than to the centre.”
args.against: “And the kite flew straight for two hours on Saturday, before it was left out on the grass overnight.”

clears: Gusty wind: “The breeze has held steady from the west at nine miles an hour all week.”
A torn covering: “Both sides of the covering are intact, with no tear, hole or split seam anywhere.”
d.note: Three faults all pull the same corner down, and all three date from the same weekend. The tail is the one with a timing problem, since it was already short on Saturday evening and the kite flew straight for two hours. Whether that clears it depends on when those two hours actually were, and the text does not say.

title: The Case of the Pots That Stayed Wet
story: The shamrock seedlings on the back shelf are in trouble in three ways at once. Every stem leans hard toward the door. The leaves have faded from deep green to a yellowish pale. And the compost is still soaking four days after watering, when it used to dry out in two. Overwatering makes soil wet, but it does not make a plant lean, and the pots get the same cup each Monday. Poor compost gives weak growth from the start, and these were strong for five weeks. Cold would slow them without bending them toward one side of the room. A pest in the soil chews roots and wilts a plant, and nothing here is wilting. The sycamore outside the window came into full leaf in the third week of April. The shelf has had deep shade since, and the only bright thing in the room is the open door. A plant in poor light grows toward the brightest thing it can find and thins its colour. A plant in poor light also works slowly, drinks little, and leaves its pot wet.
q: What is wrong with the seedlings?

sus.why: the sycamore outside the window came into full leaf in the third week of April, and the shelf has had deep shade since
overwatering makes soil wet, but it does not make a plant lean, and the pots get the same cup each Monday
poor compost gives weak growth from the start, and these were strong for five weeks
cold would slow them without bending them toward one side of the room
a pest in the soil chews roots and wilts a plant, and nothing here is wilting

ans: The tree outside has put the shelf into deep shade.
proof: “The shelf has had deep shade since, and the only bright thing in the room is the open door.”
“A plant in poor light grows toward the brightest thing it can find and thins its colour.”
“A plant in poor light also works slowly, drinks little, and leaves its pot wet.”
clears: Overwatering: “it does not make a plant lean, and the pots get the same cup each Monday.”
The compost: “these were strong for five weeks.”
Cold: “would slow them without bending them toward one side of the room.”
A pest: “nothing here is wilting.”
explain: Wet soil looks like a watering mistake until you notice that nothing about the watering changed and the stems are pointing at the door. Shade explains the leaning, the pale colour and the wet pot together, because a plant that cannot work does not drink.

d.story: The shamrock seedlings on the back shelf are in trouble in three ways at once. Every stem leans hard toward the door. The leaves have faded from deep green to a yellowish pale. And the compost is still soaking four days after watering, when it used to dry out in two. The sycamore outside the window came into full leaf in the third week of April. The shelf has had deep shade since, and the only bright thing in the room is the open door. A plant in poor light grows toward the brightest thing it can find and thins its colour. The Monday cup was swapped in April for the new can, which pours three times as much. Roots standing in water rot, and a rotted root cannot hold its stem upright. A stem with no strength left falls toward the only gap along the shelf, which is the door end. The back shelf stands against the outside wall, and the thermometer on it reads eleven degrees. The compost came from the same bag as the window trays, which are thriving. Every pot has been tipped out and checked, and no grub, worm or egg was found.
d.q: What is wrong with the seedlings? Pick one cause and prove it from the text.

sus.why: a sycamore in full leaf since April, putting the shelf in deep shade
a Monday cup swapped in April for a can pouring three times as much
the same bag of compost as the window trays, which are thriving
eleven degrees on an outside wall, with warm air at the door
every pot tipped out, with no grub, worm or egg found

evidence: “The sycamore outside the window came into full leaf in the third week of April.”
“The shelf has had deep shade since, and the only bright thing in the room is the open door.”
args.against: “Warm air from the corridor comes in through that same open door all morning.”

evidence: “The Monday cup was swapped in April for the new can, which pours three times as much.”
“Roots standing in water rot, and a rotted root cannot hold its stem upright.”
args.against: “The leaves have faded from deep green to a yellowish pale.”

evidence: “The back shelf stands against the outside wall, and the thermometer on it reads eleven degrees.”
“Warm air from the corridor comes in through that same open door all morning.”
args.against: “A plant in poor light grows toward the brightest thing it can find and thins its colour.”

clears: Poor compost: “The compost came from the same bag as the window trays, which are thriving.”
A pest in the soil: “Every pot has been tipped out and checked, and no grub, worm or egg was found.”
d.note: The open door is both the bright thing and the warm thing, so the lean points at two suspects at once and cannot tell them apart. The faded colour is what light explains and cold does not, and the wet compost is what cold explains at least as well. Ask which symptom a class is willing to call the most diagnostic, and why.

title: The Case of the Puddle in Dry Weather
story: A puddle the size of a table sits in the middle of the new playground, and it has not rained for nine days. Two further details have been noted in the site book and left there. A faint white ring has dried onto the tarmac around its edge. And the water in it is slightly warm to the hand, even first thing in the morning. Rain is the obvious source, and the gauge by the fence has recorded nothing since the eleventh. The downpipe from the roof empties twenty metres away and the ground between is dust. A dip in the tarmac would hold rainwater and then dry out like every other dip in the yard. Children emptying bottles would make a cold puddle that is gone within an hour. A heating pipe runs under that corner of the playground from the boiler house. Water escaping from it arrives warm and keeps arriving whatever the weather does. Mains water carries dissolved minerals, and a puddle that evaporates at its edges leaves them behind as a pale ring. The puddle has been the same size every morning for nine days.
q: Where is the water coming from?

sus.why: a heating pipe runs under that corner of the playground, and water escaping from it arrives warm
the gauge by the fence has recorded nothing since the eleventh
the downpipe from the roof empties twenty metres away and the ground between is dust
a dip in the tarmac would hold rainwater and then dry out like every other dip in the yard
children emptying bottles would make a cold puddle that is gone within an hour

ans: A heating pipe under the playground is leaking.
proof: “Water escaping from it arrives warm and keeps arriving whatever the weather does.”
“Mains water carries dissolved minerals, and a puddle that evaporates at its edges leaves them behind as a pale ring.”
“The puddle has been the same size every morning for nine days.”
clears: Rain: “the gauge by the fence has recorded nothing since the eleventh.”
The downpipe: “empties twenty metres away and the ground between is dust.”
A dip: “would hold rainwater and then dry out like every other dip in the yard.”
Bottles: “would make a cold puddle that is gone within an hour.”
explain: A puddle that will not dry, a mineral ring and warm water are three answers to three different questions: where the water comes from, how long it has been arriving, and how hot it was when it did. Only a buried heating pipe answers all three with one sentence.

d.story: A puddle the size of a table sits in the middle of the new playground, and it has not rained for nine days. Two further details have been noted in the site book and left there. A faint white ring has dried onto the tarmac around its edge. And the water in it is slightly warm to the hand, even first thing in the morning. A heating pipe runs under that corner of the playground from the boiler house. Water escaping from it arrives warm and keeps arriving whatever the weather does. The downpipe was rerouted in September into a soakaway that was never finished. It ends six metres away, under the new tarmac, and it drains the boiler house roof. That roof runs warm for an hour after every firing, and the water off it comes down warm. The tarmac over this corner has sunk four centimetres since the summer, which is the deepest hollow in the yard. The trench dug for the pipe was backfilled loose, and loose ground settles and lets groundwater rise. Mains and ground water both carry dissolved minerals, and a puddle that evaporates at its edges leaves a pale ring. The rain gauge by the fence has recorded nothing at all since the eleventh. No bottle has been allowed on the playground since the new rule in September.
d.q: Where is the puddle coming from? Pick one source and prove it from the text.

sus.why: a heating pipe running under that corner from the boiler house
a rain gauge recording nothing at all since the eleventh
a downpipe rerouted into an unfinished soakaway six metres away
tarmac sunk four centimetres over a loosely backfilled trench
no bottles on the playground since the September rule

evidence: “A heating pipe runs under that corner of the playground from the boiler house.”
“Water escaping from it arrives warm and keeps arriving whatever the weather does.”
args.against: “The tarmac over this corner has sunk four centimetres since the summer, which is the deepest hollow in the yard.”

evidence: “The downpipe was rerouted in September into a soakaway that was never finished.”
“It ends six metres away, under the new tarmac, and it drains the boiler house roof.”
args.against: “The rain gauge by the fence has recorded nothing at all since the eleventh.”

evidence: “The tarmac over this corner has sunk four centimetres since the summer, which is the deepest hollow in the yard.”
“The trench dug for the pipe was backfilled loose, and loose ground settles and lets groundwater rise.”
args.against: “And the water in it is slightly warm to the hand, even first thing in the morning.”

clears: Rain: “The rain gauge by the fence has recorded nothing at all since the eleventh.”
Spilled bottles: “No bottle has been allowed on the playground since the new rule in September.”
d.note: Warmth used to belong to the heating pipe alone. A downpipe off a warm roof takes that away, and a hollow over the pipe trench gets warmth from below for free. The nine days without rain is the fact that hurts the downpipe answer, and a class should be asked to say so rather than let it slide.

title: The Case of the Strip Where Nothing Grew
story: A strip about a metre wide runs across the school garden and nothing will grow on it. Two more things are true of that strip and of no other part of the plot. The soil in it is pale grey and sets into a crust after every watering. And even the weeds stop at its edge, though they are thick on both sides of it. Shade would stunt the beans without stopping dandelions, which grow happily in shade. Slugs eat leaves and leave stems and roots, and there are no chewed leaves anywhere on the strip. Uneven watering would show as wilting plants rather than bare ground. A buried path would be hard and shallow, and a fork goes into this strip easily enough. The builders washed out the cement mixer on that line every evening last summer. Cement washings are strongly alkaline, and the test strip pushed into the strip reads nine. Most garden plants take up nothing at that reading, however good the soil looks. Fine cement particles also fill the gaps between soil grains and set when they dry.
q: Why is the strip bare?

sus.why: the builders washed out the cement mixer on that line every evening last summer
shade would stunt the beans without stopping dandelions, which grow happily in shade
slugs eat leaves and leave stems and roots, and there are no chewed leaves anywhere on the strip
uneven watering would show as wilting plants rather than bare ground
a buried path would be hard and shallow, and a fork goes into this strip easily enough

ans: Cement washings have made the strip too alkaline for anything.
proof: “Cement washings are strongly alkaline, and the test strip pushed into the strip reads nine.”
“Most garden plants take up nothing at that reading, however good the soil looks.”
“Fine cement particles also fill the gaps between soil grains and set when they dry.”
clears: Shade: “would stunt the beans without stopping dandelions, which grow happily in shade.”
Slugs: “there are no chewed leaves anywhere on the strip.”
Watering: “would show as wilting plants rather than bare ground.”
A path: “a fork goes into this strip easily enough.”
explain: A bare strip, grey crusting soil, and weeds that stop dead at a line. Shade and slugs and watering each leave something growing. The mixer explains the chemistry, the colour and the crust at once, and it explains the shape, because a man rinsing a drum walks the same line every evening.

d.story: A strip about a metre wide runs across the school garden and nothing will grow on it. Two more things are true of that strip and of no other part of the plot. The soil in it is pale grey and sets into a crust after every watering. And even the weeds stop at its edge, though they are thick on both sides of it. The builders washed out the cement mixer on that line every evening last summer. Cement washings are strongly alkaline, and a test strip pushed into the soil there reads nine. Most garden plants take up nothing at that reading, however good the soil looks. The leaking joint in the sprinkler line sits over this strip and floods it every evening. Ground that never drains goes grey and airless, and roots drown in it. Tap water left to evaporate on a surface leaves its own pale crust behind. A trial pit found a band of hard hoggin thirty centimetres down, on the line of the old path. Roots that reach that band stop, and a metre-wide path is a metre-wide strip. The strip lies in full sun from ten in the morning until the wall shades the far bed. Not one leaf on the plot, inside the strip or outside it, has been chewed this year.
d.q: Why will nothing grow on the strip? Choose one cause and quote the text.

sus.why: a mixer washed out on that line every evening last summer
full sun from ten until the wall shades the far bed
no chewed leaf anywhere on the plot this year
a sprinkler joint leaking over the strip every evening
a band of hard hoggin thirty centimetres down, a metre wide

evidence: “The builders washed out the cement mixer on that line every evening last summer.”
“Cement washings are strongly alkaline, and a test strip pushed into the soil there reads nine.”
args.against: “A trial pit found a band of hard hoggin thirty centimetres down, on the line of the old path.”

evidence: “The leaking joint in the sprinkler line sits over this strip and floods it every evening.”
“Ground that never drains goes grey and airless, and roots drown in it.”
args.against: “Most garden plants take up nothing at that reading, however good the soil looks.”

evidence: “A trial pit found a band of hard hoggin thirty centimetres down, on the line of the old path.”
“Roots that reach that band stop, and a metre-wide path is a metre-wide strip.”
args.against: “The soil in it is pale grey and sets into a crust after every watering.”

clears: Shade: “The strip lies in full sun from ten in the morning until the wall shades the far bed.”
Slugs: “Not one leaf on the plot, inside the strip or outside it, has been chewed this year.”
d.note: Three different things are a metre wide and in the same line, because the builders worked along the old path and the sprinkler was laid in the same trench. Grey soil and a crust now have three explanations, and the pH reading of nine is the only measurement in the case. Ask what the other two answers would need measured to match it.

title: The Case of the Hens That Pecked the Wall
story: The school hens are laying eggs so thin that half of them crack in the collecting box. Two other changes have been written in the keepers' diary as separate worries. The birds have started breaking and eating their own eggs in the nest. And they spend part of every morning pecking at the old lime mortar between the bricks of the coop wall. Age thins a shell gradually over years, and these four hens are eighteen months old and were fine in March. Cold slows laying rather than thinning what is laid. A new bird in the flock causes fighting, and no bird has been added since last spring. Disease would show in the hens themselves, and the vet found four healthy birds. The feed was changed in April to a cheaper brand without added shell grit. The grit hopper has stood empty since, because the old feed made it unnecessary. A hen with too little calcium cannot build a thick shell, so she lays a thin one. She will also go looking for calcium wherever she can find it, and lime mortar is calcium.
q: What is behind all three changes?

sus.why: the feed was changed in April to a cheaper brand without added shell grit, and the grit hopper has stood empty since
age thins a shell gradually over years, and these four hens are eighteen months old and were fine in March
cold slows laying rather than thinning what is laid
a new bird in the flock causes fighting, and no bird has been added since last spring
disease would show in the hens themselves, and the vet found four healthy birds

ans: The new feed has no calcium in it and the grit hopper is empty.
proof: “The grit hopper has stood empty since, because the old feed made it unnecessary.”
“A hen with too little calcium cannot build a thick shell, so she lays a thin one.”
“She will also go looking for calcium wherever she can find it, and lime mortar is calcium.”
clears: Age: “these four hens are eighteen months old and were fine in March.”
Cold: “cold slows laying rather than thinning what is laid.”
A new bird: “no bird has been added since last spring.”
Disease: “the vet found four healthy birds.”
explain: Thin shells, egg eating and a pecked wall were three entries on three pages. They are one hunger. A hen short of calcium makes a poor shell and then goes after calcium anywhere she can reach it, which is her own broken egg and the lime in the mortar.

d.story: The school hens are laying eggs so thin that half of them crack in the collecting box. Two other changes have been written in the keepers' diary as separate worries. The birds have started breaking and eating their own eggs in the nest. And they spend part of every morning pecking at the old lime mortar between the bricks of the coop wall. The feed was changed in April to a cheaper brand without added shell grit. The grit hopper has stood empty since, because the old feed made it unnecessary. A hen with too little calcium lays a thin shell and goes looking for calcium anywhere she can find it. The coop lost half its roofing felt in the March gales and has not been patched. A hen spending her food on keeping warm has little left over for building a shell. Cold birds eat constantly and will try anything that tastes of mineral. The vet's droppings sample came back in May with a heavy worm burden in all four birds. Worms take calcium out of the gut before a hen can use any of it. All four hens are eighteen months old, which is the first year of a hen's best laying. No bird has joined or left this flock since the four of them arrived together last spring.
d.q: Why are the shells so thin? Pick one cause and prove it from the diary.

sus.why: a cheaper feed since April and a grit hopper standing empty
eighteen months old, in the first year of best laying
half the roofing felt gone since the March gales
the same four birds since last spring, none joining or leaving
a May sample showing a heavy worm burden in all four

evidence: “The feed was changed in April to a cheaper brand without added shell grit.”
“The grit hopper has stood empty since, because the old feed made it unnecessary.”
args.against: “Worms take calcium out of the gut before a hen can use any of it.”

evidence: “The coop lost half its roofing felt in the March gales and has not been patched.”
“A hen spending her food on keeping warm has little left over for building a shell.”
args.against: “And they spend part of every morning pecking at the old lime mortar between the bricks of the coop wall.”

evidence: “The vet's droppings sample came back in May with a heavy worm burden in all four birds.”
“Worms take calcium out of the gut before a hen can use any of it.”
args.against: “The feed was changed in April to a cheaper brand without added shell grit.”

clears: The hens' age: “All four hens are eighteen months old, which is the first year of a hen's best laying.”
A new bird: “No bird has joined or left this flock since the four of them arrived together last spring.”
d.note: All three open answers end at the same place, which is a hen short of calcium, and they disagree about where the calcium went. That is a better argument than a wrong one, and the mortar pecking supports every one of them equally. The March roof is the only one that comes before April, and dates are what this case is really about.

title: The Case of the Rejected Recycling
story: The paper recycling has been refused by the collectors three weeks running, and two other facts have gone in the log unconnected. The bin now takes two people to wheel out when one managed it all last year. And there is standing water four centimetres deep in the bottom of it. Wrong items in the bin get a load rejected, and the audit on Monday found nothing in it but paper and card. A new collector with new rules would have said so, and the crew and the contract are unchanged. A bin too small would overflow rather than fail inspection. The paper itself comes from the same three classrooms it always came from. The bin lid has been propped open with a brick since the handle broke in February. Rain has gone straight in every week since, and a wheeled bin has no drain. Wet paper weighs several times what dry paper weighs, which is the whole difference in the wheeling. And a mill cannot take pulp that has already been soaked and begun to rot, so the load is refused at the gate.
q: Why does the recycling keep getting refused?

sus.why: the bin lid has been propped open with a brick since the handle broke in February, and rain has gone straight in
the audit on Monday found nothing in it but paper and card
a new collector with new rules would have said so, and the crew and the contract are unchanged
a bin too small would overflow rather than fail inspection
the paper itself comes from the same three classrooms it always came from

ans: The propped lid has let rain soak the paper since February.
proof: “Rain has gone straight in every week since, and a wheeled bin has no drain.”
“Wet paper weighs several times what dry paper weighs, which is the whole difference in the wheeling.”
“And a mill cannot take pulp that has already been soaked and begun to rot, so the load is refused at the gate.”
clears: Wrong items: “the audit on Monday found nothing in it but paper and card.”
The collector: “the crew and the contract are unchanged.”
A small bin: “would overflow rather than fail inspection.”
The classrooms: “the paper itself comes from the same three classrooms it always came from.”
explain: A refused load points at what went into the bin. Nothing wrong went in. What went in was rain, through a lid held open since February, and that one brick accounts for the weight, the water in the bottom and the refusal, because soaked paper is no longer paper to a mill.

d.story: The paper recycling has been refused by the collectors three weeks running, and two other facts have gone in the log unconnected. The bin now takes two people to wheel out when one managed it all last year. And there is standing water four centimetres deep in the bottom of it. The bin lid has been propped open with a brick since the handle broke in February. Rain has gone straight in every week since, and a wheeled bin has no drain. Wet paper weighs several times what dry paper weighs, which is the whole difference in the wheeling. Monday's audit went one bag deep and stopped there. Nothing below that bag has been looked at since February, and a kitchen sack was seen going in during March. One sack of food waste in a load is enough for a mill to refuse the lot at the gate. Room six moved its paint-washing trays beside the bin in February. The soaked paper towels from those trays have gone in with the class paper every day since. A load that arrives wet and rotting is turned away whatever else is in it. The crew, the lorry and the contract are all the same ones as last year. The bin is the large size and has never once been filled to its lid.
d.q: Why is the recycling being refused? Choose one cause and quote the log.

sus.why: a lid propped open with a brick since February
an audit that went one bag deep and stopped
the same crew, lorry and contract as last year
a bin of the large size, never once filled to its lid
paint-washing trays moved beside the bin in February

evidence: “The bin lid has been propped open with a brick since the handle broke in February.”
“Rain has gone straight in every week since, and a wheeled bin has no drain.”
args.against: “The soaked paper towels from those trays have gone in with the class paper every day since.”

evidence: “Monday's audit went one bag deep and stopped there.”
“Nothing below that bag has been looked at since February, and a kitchen sack was seen going in during March.”
args.against: “And there is standing water four centimetres deep in the bottom of it.”

evidence: “Room six moved its paint-washing trays beside the bin in February.”
“The soaked paper towels from those trays have gone in with the class paper every day since.”
args.against: “Rain has gone straight in every week since, and a wheeled bin has no drain.”

clears: A new collector: “The crew, the lorry and the contract are all the same ones as last year.”
A bin too small: “The bin is the large size and has never once been filled to its lid.”
d.note: An audit one bag deep is the sentence this case is built on. It is exactly how a real inspection goes wrong, and it turns a clean result into no result at all. Students who spot that the audit proves nothing about the bottom of the bin have learned more than the ones who pick the right answer.

title: The Case of the Haze in the Corner
story: Every photograph taken on the school camera since the trip has a soft grey haze across the upper left corner. Two other facts were mentioned at the time and forgotten. The haze is almost invisible indoors and very strong whenever the camera points anywhere near the sun. And the camera bag smells of coconut, because a bottle of sun cream burst in it on the coach. A scratched lens shows as a hard bright line that looks the same in any light. Dust on the sensor makes small dark specks in fixed places, not a soft wash of grey. The strap in front of the lens appears as a sharp dark shape, and nothing here has an edge. A fault in the camera would mark every picture equally whatever the light was doing. A thin film of grease sits across one corner of the front element. Grease does not block light, it scatters it, which is why the mark is soft and grey. Scattering needs strong light to show, so a bright sky makes it obvious and a classroom hides it. The film is in the corner the burst bottle lay against.
q: What is making the haze?

sus.why: a thin film of grease sits across one corner of the front element, in the corner the burst bottle lay against
a scratched lens shows as a hard bright line that looks the same in any light
dust on the sensor makes small dark specks in fixed places, not a soft wash of grey
the strap in front of the lens appears as a sharp dark shape, and nothing here has an edge
a fault in the camera would mark every picture equally whatever the light was doing

ans: A film of spilled sun cream is smeared on one corner of the lens.
proof: “Grease does not block light, it scatters it, which is why the mark is soft and grey.”
“Scattering needs strong light to show, so a bright sky makes it obvious and a classroom hides it.”
“The film is in the corner the burst bottle lay against.”
clears: A scratch: “shows as a hard bright line that looks the same in any light.”
Sensor dust: “makes small dark specks in fixed places, not a soft wash of grey.”
The strap: “appears as a sharp dark shape, and nothing here has an edge.”
A camera fault: “would mark every picture equally whatever the light was doing.”
explain: The mark has three properties: it is soft, it is in one corner, and it only shows against the light. Grease supplies all three, because it scatters rather than blocks, it sits where it was spilled, and scattering is invisible until there is plenty of light to scatter.

d.story: Every photograph taken on the school camera since the trip has a soft grey haze across the upper left corner. Two other facts were mentioned at the time and forgotten. The haze is almost invisible indoors and very strong whenever the camera points anywhere near the sun. And the camera bag smells of coconut, because a bottle of sun cream burst in it on the coach. A thin film of grease sits across one corner of the front element, where the burst bottle lay against it. Grease does not block light, it scatters it, which is why the mark is soft and grey. The same corner of that element carries a web of fine scratches from being wiped with a dry sleeve. A thousand small scratches scatter light exactly as a film does, and show only against a bright sky. The camera was dropped on the coach steps the same afternoon the bottle burst. Its lens barrel no longer seats square, and there is a gap at the upper left of the mount. Light entering a mount from outside washes the frame nearest that gap and needs a bright sun to do it. The sensor was cleaned and checked by the shop in the week after the trip. The strap has been clipped to the right-hand lug alone since the left clip was lost.
d.q: What is hazing the corner? Pick one cause and prove it from the text.

sus.why: a film of grease where the burst bottle lay against the lens
a web of fine scratches in the same corner of the element
a sensor cleaned and checked by the shop after the trip
a strap clipped to the right-hand lug alone
a barrel that no longer seats square, gapping at the upper left

evidence: “A thin film of grease sits across one corner of the front element, where the burst bottle lay against it.”
“Grease does not block light, it scatters it, which is why the mark is soft and grey.”

title: The Case of the Brown Leaf Tips
story: The six spider plants on the classroom bookcase have dry brown tips on every leaf. Two other things are true of those six and not of the four on the windowsill. A hard white crust has formed across the top of their compost. And their saucers have never been emptied, while the windowsill saucers are tipped out each Friday. All ten plants get the same water from the same can on the same day. Dry air would brown the windowsill plants too, and they sit closer to the radiator than the bookcase does. Too little water leaves a plant limp and its compost light, and these pots are heavy and damp. Too much sun scorches whole patches of leaf rather than the last centimetre of each tip. Tap water carries dissolved salts, and the water leaves but the salts do not. A pot standing in its own drainage takes that water back up, salts and all. Salt gathers at the far end of a leaf, which is the tip, and burns it. The crust on the compost is the same salt, left where the surface dried.
q: Why do only six plants have brown tips?

dry air would brown the windowsill plants too, and they sit closer to the radiator than the bookcase does
too little water leaves a plant limp and its compost light, and these pots are heavy and damp
too much sun scorches whole patches of leaf rather than the last centimetre of each tip
all ten plants get the same water from the same can on the same day

ans: The six pots keep drinking their own salty drainage back.
proof: “Tap water carries dissolved salts, and the water leaves but the salts do not.”
“Salt gathers at the far end of a leaf, which is the tip, and burns it.”
“The crust on the compost is the same salt, left where the surface dried.”
clears: Dry air: “they sit closer to the radiator than the bookcase does.”
Too little water: “these pots are heavy and damp.”
Too much sun: “scorches whole patches of leaf rather than the last centimetre of each tip.”
The can: “all ten plants get the same water from the same can on the same day.”
explain: Four plants on the windowsill get the same water and are fine, so the water is not the difference. The difference is what happens after it drains. Salt left in a saucer goes back up the pot, builds a crust on top and burns the tip of every leaf, which is three symptoms from one habit.

title: The Case of the Gritty Ice Cream
story: Ice cream from the chest freezer in the kitchen is gritty with ice crystals however new the tub is. Two other facts have been mentioned to the caretaker and never followed up. There is a hard sheet of frost two centimetres thick across the underside of the lid. And the freezer's compressor now runs almost continuously instead of switching on and off. An old tub would explain a gritty one, and the tub opened on Friday was bought that morning. A poor brand would be gritty from the first spoonful, and the first spoonful of this one was smooth. A freezer set too warm would show on the thermometer, and it reads minus nineteen degrees. Overfilling slows the cold air, and the freezer is half empty. The rubber seal along the front edge has a notch cut out of it the width of a thumb. Warm damp air leaks in through that notch all day and the cold leaks out, which is why the motor never stops. Water from that air freezes on the first cold surface it meets, which is the lid. And ice cream that part thaws and refreezes grows the big crystals you can feel on the tongue.
q: What is ruining the ice cream?

sus.why: the rubber seal along the front edge has a notch cut out of it the width of a thumb
an old tub would explain a gritty one, and the tub opened on Friday was bought that morning
a poor brand would be gritty from the first spoonful, and the first spoonful of this one was smooth
a freezer set too warm would show on the thermometer, and it reads minus nineteen degrees
overfilling slows the cold air, and the freezer is half empty

ans: A notch in the door seal is letting warm damp air in.
proof: “Warm damp air leaks in through that notch all day and the cold leaks out, which is why the motor never stops.”
“Water from that air freezes on the first cold surface it meets, which is the lid.”
“And ice cream that part thaws and refreezes grows the big crystals you can feel on the tongue.”
clears: An old tub: “the tub opened on Friday was bought that morning.”
A poor brand: “the first spoonful of this one was smooth.”
A warm setting: “it reads minus nineteen degrees.”
Overfilling: “the freezer is half empty.”
explain: The thermometer says the freezer is cold enough, so the temperature looks innocent. It is the only reading taken, and it is taken in one place at one moment. A notch in the seal explains the frost, the motor that never rests, and the crystals, because all three are what leaking air does.

title: The Case of the Ribbons That Turned Pink
story: Half the charity ribbons on the entrance noticeboard have faded from deep red to a washed-out pink. Two other facts about the board belong with that one. The faded ribbons are all on the left half, and the line between faded and unfaded is straight and sharp. And the backing paper under the left half has yellowed while the right half is still white. A bad batch of dye would fade ribbons wherever they happened to be pinned. Rain cannot reach a board in a dry entrance hall with no window above it. The radiator below the board heats the bottom row hardest, and the bottom row on the right is as red as the day it was pinned. Handling wears a ribbon at its edges rather than taking the colour out of the middle. A ribbon from the same box, kept in the office drawer since October, is still deep red. The high window over the door throws a hard-edged block of sunlight onto the left half of the board every afternoon. Sunlight breaks down dye, which is fading, and it yellows paper, which is ageing. Both happen only where the light lands, and light lands in straight-edged shapes.
q: Why did half the ribbons fade?

sus.why: the high window over the door throws a hard-edged block of sunlight onto the left half of the board every afternoon
a bad batch of dye would fade ribbons wherever they happened to be pinned
rain cannot reach a board in a dry entrance hall with no window above it
the bottom row on the right is as red as the day it was pinned
handling wears a ribbon at its edges rather than taking the colour out of the middle

ans: Afternoon sun falls on the left half of the board.
proof: “Sunlight breaks down dye, which is fading, and it yellows paper, which is ageing.”
“Both happen only where the light lands, and light lands in straight-edged shapes.”
“A ribbon from the same box, kept in the office drawer since October, is still deep red.”
clears: The dye: “would fade ribbons wherever they happened to be pinned.”
Rain: “rain cannot reach a board in a dry entrance hall with no window above it.”
The radiator: “the bottom row on the right is as red as the day it was pinned.”
Handling: “wears a ribbon at its edges rather than taking the colour out of the middle.”
explain: A straight line across a noticeboard is not something dye or damp or hands can draw. Light can. It explains the shape, the faded ribbons and the yellowed paper in one go, and the ribbon shut in a drawer since October proves the box was never the problem.

title: The Case of the Balloons That Came Back Up
story: Forty balloons tied for the leavers' assembly were lying on the floor when the caretaker opened the hall at seven. Two other facts from that morning were noticed and nobody made anything of them. The dog bowl by the kitchen door had a skin of ice on it. And by half past eleven most of the balloons were floating again, without anyone touching them. A leak lets gas out and there is no way back in, so a leaking balloon stays down. Underfilled balloons would never have flown, and these flew all through Thursday afternoon. Ribbons too heavy for the lift would have dragged them down on Thursday as well. A punctured balloon goes soft and wrinkled, and all forty are tight and smooth. The hall heating was off overnight and the room fell close to freezing. Gas shrinks as it cools, so each balloon held a smaller volume of helium by morning. A smaller balloon pushes aside less air, and it is the pushed-aside air that lifts it. Warming the hall through the morning let the gas expand again and the lift came back with it.
q: Why did the balloons sink and then rise?

sus.why: the hall heating was off overnight and the room fell close to freezing, and gas shrinks as it cools
a leak lets gas out and there is no way back in, so a leaking balloon stays down
underfilled balloons would never have flown, and these flew all through Thursday afternoon
ribbons too heavy for the lift would have dragged them down on Thursday as well
a punctured balloon goes soft and wrinkled, and all forty are tight and smooth

ans: The cold shrank the helium overnight and the warmth gave it back.
proof: “Gas shrinks as it cools, so each balloon held a smaller volume of helium by morning.”
“A smaller balloon pushes aside less air, and it is the pushed-aside air that lifts it.”
“Warming the hall through the morning let the gas expand again and the lift came back with it.”
clears: A leak: “there is no way back in, so a leaking balloon stays down.”
Underfilled: “these flew all through Thursday afternoon.”
Heavy ribbons: “would have dragged them down on Thursday as well.”
A puncture: “all forty are tight and smooth.”
explain: Everything that takes gas out of a balloon is permanent, so the balloons coming back up on their own rules all of it out at once. Only a change that can reverse fits, and the ice on the dog bowl says what the change was. One cold night explains the fall, the ice and the recovery.
